items.title: NISM V-A Investment Landscape: Revision Notes
items.description: Revise savings vs investment, asset classes, real return, risk types and financial planning basics for the NISM Series V-A mutual fund distributor exam.
items.intro: This opening chapter of the NISM V-A workbook sets the stage: why households must invest rather than merely save, which asset classes exist in India, and what risks each carries. Questions are mostly conceptual, with a few quick calculations on real return, compounding and the effect of inflation. Expect scenario questions that ask which asset suits a described investor.

points.heading: Saving versus investing
points.text: Saving is setting aside part of income; investing is deploying those savings so they earn a return. Money kept in a savings account at 3% while inflation runs at 5% is losing purchasing power every year, which is the core argument the workbook uses for investing.

points.heading: Physical and financial assets
points.text: Physical (real) assets include land, a flat, gold jewellery and commodities. Financial assets are claims on an issuer: shares, bonds, bank deposits, mutual fund units and insurance policies. A rented flat is a real asset; a bank FD is a financial asset even though it feels equally 'safe'.

points.heading: Equity as an asset class
points.text: Equity gives part-ownership of a company. Returns come from dividends and capital appreciation, both uncertain. Equity has the highest long-term growth potential among mainstream assets but also the highest short-term volatility, so it suits long horizons such as retirement 20 years away.

points.heading: Debt as an asset class
points.text: Debt instruments (bonds, debentures, deposits, T-bills, commercial paper) promise interest and repayment of principal. Key risks are credit risk (issuer default) and interest rate risk (prices fall when rates rise). Government securities carry negligible credit risk but still carry interest rate risk.

points.heading: Gold, real estate and alternatives
points.text: Gold is a hedge against currency weakness and crises and has no regular income. Real estate needs large ticket sizes, is illiquid and carries high transaction costs such as stamp duty. Alternatives include REITs, InvITs, AIFs and structured products, usually for more experienced investors.

points.heading: Nominal and real return
points.text: Nominal return is what the instrument pays; real return adjusts for inflation. An FD at 7% with 5% inflation gives a real return of roughly 2%. Precisely, (1.07/1.05) - 1 = 1.9%. Exams usually accept the approximate subtraction. Negative real returns are common on savings accounts.

points.heading: Main investment risks
points.text: Inflation risk erodes purchasing power; liquidity risk means you cannot sell quickly at a fair price; credit risk is default; interest rate risk hits bond prices; market risk affects all equities; reinvestment risk arises when coupons must be reinvested at lower rates.

points.heading: Liquidity and marketability
points.text: Liquidity is how quickly an asset turns into cash without loss of value. A savings account is highly liquid; a flat may take months to sell and may need a price cut. An open-ended fund is liquid because the AMC redeems units at NAV.

points.heading: Diversification
points.text: Spreading money across companies, sectors and asset classes reduces unsystematic (company-specific) risk. It cannot remove systematic risk such as a market-wide fall after an interest rate shock. Owning 30 stocks across sectors is diversified; 30 bank stocks is not. Asset-class diversification adds a further cushion.

points.heading: Life cycle and goals
points.text: A young earner can take more equity risk because of a long horizon and steady income; a retiree needs regular income and capital safety. Financial planning links each goal - house, child's education, retirement - to an amount, a date and a suitable asset mix.

formulas: Real return (approx) = Nominal return - Inflation rate
Exact real return = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1
Future value = Present value x (1 + r)^n, where r is the annual rate and n the number of years
traps: Calling a bank FD or debt fund a 'real asset' - real assets are physical; every deposit, bond or unit is a financial asset.
Assuming government bonds have no risk: they are free of credit risk but their prices still fall when interest rates rise.
Mixing up diversification's effect: it reduces company-specific risk, never the market-wide systematic risk.
Forgetting that liquidity and safety differ: a listed small-cap share can be liquid yet highly risky.
items.recap: Invest, don't just save, because inflation eats idle money. Real assets are physical; financial assets are claims. Equity grows most but swings most; debt carries credit and interest rate risk; gold hedges crises. Real return is roughly nominal minus inflation. Diversification cuts only unsystematic risk. Match the asset to the goal and the horizon.

items.chapter: Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund
items.title: Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund: NISM V-A Notes
items.description: Pooling, units and NAV, open vs closed-ended schemes, SEBI fund categories and the benefits and limits of mutual funds explained for NISM V-A revision.
items.intro: This chapter explains what a mutual fund is, how units and NAV work, the main scheme types and SEBI's categorisation, and why funds suit retail investors. It is one of the most heavily tested chapters in V-A, with many direct questions on scheme categories and their minimum allocations, plus questions contrasting open-ended, closed-ended and interval schemes.

points.heading: Pooling and units
points.text: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it per a stated objective. Investors receive units; each unit represents a proportionate share of the scheme's net assets. If you hold 1% of the units you own 1% of the portfolio, gains and losses alike.

points.heading: Benefits for small investors
points.text: Professional management, diversification with a small amount (SIPs can start at a few hundred rupees), liquidity in open-ended schemes, transparency through daily NAV and monthly portfolio disclosure, and SEBI regulation. A ₹500 SIP buys a slice of 50+ stocks. Each investor's holding is shown in a single statement.

points.heading: Limitations
points.text: No control over the portfolio, costs through the expense ratio, returns that are not assured, and possible over-diversification. Investors also cannot tailor holdings for their own tax position. Funds are market-linked: NAV can fall below the purchase price. Exit loads and taxes can also reduce net returns.

points.heading: Open-ended, closed-ended, interval
points.text: Open-ended schemes allow purchase and redemption on every business day at NAV-based prices. Closed-ended schemes have a fixed maturity; investors exit before maturity only by selling on the stock exchange where units are compulsorily listed. Interval schemes open for transactions only during specified intervals.

points.heading: Active versus passive
points.text: Active funds try to beat a benchmark through stock selection and carry higher expense ratios. Passive funds - index funds and ETFs - replicate an index and aim for minimal tracking error, not outperformance. Lower cost is the main attraction of passive funds.

points.heading: Equity categories
points.text: SEBI's 2017 categorisation defines large cap as the top 100 companies by full market capitalisation, mid cap as 101st to 250th and small cap as 251st onwards. A large cap fund holds at least 80% in large caps; mid cap and small cap funds hold at least 65% in their segment. Multi cap needs at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps; flexi cap needs at least 65% equity with no segment limits.

points.heading: Debt categories
points.text: Debt categories are defined mainly by Macaulay duration or instrument type: overnight (1-day securities), liquid (up to 91 days maturity), ultra short, low, short, medium and long duration funds, plus money market, gilt, corporate bond, banking and PSU, credit risk and dynamic bond funds.

points.heading: Hybrid and solution-oriented
points.text: Hybrid funds mix equity and debt: conservative, balanced or aggressive hybrid, dynamic asset allocation, multi-asset (at least three asset classes) and arbitrage funds. Solution-oriented funds (retirement, children's) carry a lock-in of at least five years. ELSS has a three-year lock-in.

points.heading: Industry growth drivers
points.text: AMFI's investor awareness campaigns, the spread of SIPs, digital KYC and B-30 (beyond top 30 cities) incentives have pushed retail participation. Monthly SIP flows and folio counts are published by AMFI; quote them only from AMFI's latest data. Growth itself is not a reason to pick any particular scheme.

formulas: Large cap = top 100; Mid cap = 101-250; Small cap = 251 onwards (by full market capitalisation, list published by AMFI every six months)
traps: Confusing flexi cap (65% equity, no cap-segment minimum) with multi cap (minimum 25% each in large, mid and small cap).
Thinking investors can redeem a closed-ended scheme with the AMC before maturity - they must sell on the exchange.
Believing a passive fund tries to beat its index; it only aims to match it with low tracking error.
Assuming unit holders are lenders to the fund; they are part-owners who bear all gains and losses.
items.recap: A mutual fund pools money and issues units; NAV reflects each unit's share. Open-ended means daily liquidity; closed-ended means exchange listing for exit. Remember the cap ranks 100/250 and the minimums: large cap 80%, mid and small 65%, multi cap 25% each, flexi cap 65% equity. ELSS locks in for three years; solution-oriented funds for five.

items.title: Legal Structure of Mutual Funds in India: V-A Notes
items.description: Sponsor, trust, trustees, AMC, custodian, RTA and AMFI: revise the three-tier mutual fund structure and each entity's role for the NISM V-A exam.
items.intro: Indian mutual funds are set up as trusts with a three-tier structure of sponsor, trustees and asset management company, supported by service providers. Exam questions ask who does what: who creates the fund, who protects investors, who manages money and who holds the securities. Learn the roles and the eligibility conditions SEBI sets for each entity.

points.heading: Trust structure
points.text: A mutual fund in India is constituted as a public trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The sponsor creates the trust through a trust deed registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The trust is the mutual fund; the schemes are launched under it.

points.heading: Sponsor
points.text: The sponsor is like a promoter of a company. SEBI's eligibility criteria include a sound track record, profits in at least three of the last five years and positive net worth, with an alternative route for certain private equity sponsors. The sponsor contributes to the AMC's net worth and appoints the trustees.

points.heading: Trustees
points.text: Trustees are the investors' watchdogs. They may be individuals forming a board of trustees or a trustee company. At least two-thirds of trustees must be independent of the sponsor. They approve schemes, monitor the AMC and ensure compliance with SEBI regulations.

points.heading: Asset Management Company
points.text: The AMC is the investment manager appointed by the trustees. It designs schemes, manages portfolios, appoints most service providers and handles sales. It must maintain a minimum net worth of ₹50 crore and at least 50% of its board must be independent directors.

points.heading: Custodian
points.text: The custodian holds the scheme's securities in safekeeping, settles trades and tracks corporate actions such as dividends and bonus issues. It must be registered with SEBI. Independence matters: a sponsor and its associates cannot hold 50% or more of the custodian's voting rights if the custodian services that fund.

points.heading: Registrar and Transfer Agent
points.text: The RTA (for example CAMS or KFintech) processes purchase and redemption applications, maintains unit holder records and sends account statements. A change of address or bank mandate usually goes through the RTA or AMC, not the custodian. Investors can also submit transactions at RTA service centres.

points.heading: Other service providers
points.text: Fund accountants compute NAV, auditors audit scheme accounts (separately from the AMC's auditor), bankers handle collections and payments, and distributors bring in investors. Many functions can be outsourced, but responsibility stays with the AMC. The trustees review whether these outsourced arrangements protect unit holders adequately.

points.heading: AMFI
points.text: The Association of Mutual Funds in India is the industry body of SEBI-registered AMCs, not a regulator. It registers distributors (ARN), issues the code of conduct, runs investor awareness campaigns and publishes industry data and the market-cap list. Certification exams for distributors are conducted by NISM, not by AMFI.

points.heading: Separation of roles
points.text: The structure deliberately separates ownership of assets (trust, held by custodian), management (AMC) and oversight (trustees). This protects investors if the AMC fails: scheme assets do not belong to the AMC and cannot be used to pay its creditors. Each entity's accounts are audited independently.

traps: Mixing up trustees and the AMC: trustees supervise and protect investors, the AMC manages the money.
Calling AMFI a regulator - SEBI regulates; AMFI is a self-regulatory industry association.
Assuming the custodian maintains investor records; that is the RTA's job. The custodian holds securities.
Forgetting the ₹50 crore AMC net worth requirement and the two-thirds independence rule for trustees.
items.recap: Sponsor creates the trust; trustees (two-thirds independent) guard investors; the AMC (₹50 crore net worth, half the board independent) manages money; the custodian holds securities; the RTA keeps unit holder records. AMFI is the industry body that registers distributors. Scheme assets are held in trust, separate from the AMC's own money.

items.title: Mutual Fund Legal and Regulatory Framework: V-A Notes
items.description: SEBI's role, AMFI code of conduct, investment restrictions, investor rights and complaint routes like SCORES and SMART ODR, revised for NISM V-A.
items.intro: This chapter covers who regulates mutual funds, the investment restrictions that keep schemes diversified, AMFI's codes for AMCs and distributors, and the rights and grievance channels available to investors. Questions tend to be direct and rule-based, so memorise the escalation path for complaints and the basic investment limits.

points.heading: Role of SEBI
points.text: SEBI registers and regulates mutual funds under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, framed under the SEBI Act, 1992. It approves fund structures, lays down investment and disclosure rules, and inspects AMCs. RBI regulates money and bank-related aspects, and the stock exchanges regulate listed units, but SEBI is the primary regulator.

points.heading: Investment restrictions
points.text: SEBI limits concentration: a scheme generally cannot invest more than 10% of its NAV in equity shares of a single company (index funds and sector funds follow their own rules), and the fund as a whole cannot hold more than 10% of a company's voting capital. Debt exposure to a single issuer is capped based on rating. Check current limits with SEBI circulars.

points.heading: AMFI Code of Ethics
points.text: The AMFI Code of Ethics (ACE) sets standards of integrity, due diligence, disclosure and professional conduct for AMCs. It covers fair treatment of all investors, avoiding conflicts of interest and not making misleading statements. AMCs are expected to treat a new investor and a large institution with the same fairness, and to keep investor information confidential.

points.heading: Code of conduct for distributors
points.text: Distributors must follow AMFI's code: disclose commissions, recommend schemes suitable to the investor, avoid churning, never promise returns, and not rebate commissions. Breaches can lead to ARN suspension or cancellation. They must also keep records of client communication, update KYD details and avoid misrepresenting past performance or the risks of any scheme.

points.heading: Investor rights
points.text: Unit holders have a proportional right to the scheme's assets, the right to receive redemption proceeds within three working days for most schemes, to receive account statements and annual reports, to inspect key documents and to exit without load if fundamental attributes change.

points.heading: Investor obligations
points.text: Investors must read the scheme documents, complete KYC, provide correct details, keep records and update the folio when address, bank account or nominee changes. The workbook stresses that responsibility for investment decisions remains with the investor. Signing an application means the investor accepts the scheme's terms.

points.heading: Complaint escalation
points.text: First approach the AMC or RTA (many AMCs have an investor relations officer). If unresolved, escalate to SEBI through SCORES, the online complaints portal. After that the investor may use the SMART ODR online dispute resolution platform for conciliation and arbitration.

points.heading: Due diligence by AMCs
points.text: AMCs must carry out due diligence on distributors - checking for proper registration, business volumes and conduct - and can stop paying commissions to distributors who breach norms. The checks include the distributor's track record, any history of complaints, the number of clients served and whether its advisory and distribution roles are kept separate.

traps: Believing complaints go straight to SEBI; the AMC or RTA must be approached first, then SCORES.
Treating AMFI's code as optional guidance; breaching it can lead to cancellation of a distributor's ARN.
Saying unit holders can approve or veto every portfolio decision; they only get special rights on fundamental attribute changes.
Assuming RBI is the primary mutual fund regulator - it is SEBI.
items.recap: SEBI regulates; AMFI sets codes and registers distributors. Schemes face concentration limits such as 10% of NAV in one company's shares. Distributors must disclose commission, sell only suitable products and never promise returns. Complaints go AMC/RTA first, then SEBI SCORES, then SMART ODR. Investors may exit without load on fundamental attribute changes.

items.title: Scheme Related Information: SID, SAI and KIM Notes
items.description: Revise the Scheme Information Document, Statement of Additional Information, Key Information Memorandum, riskometer and fundamental attributes for NISM V-A.
items.intro: Investors receive several offer documents and periodic disclosures. This chapter explains what each document contains, which must accompany an application form, how the riskometer works and what counts as a fundamental attribute. Exam questions often describe a piece of information and ask which document contains it.

points.heading: Scheme Information Document
points.text: The SID contains scheme-specific details: investment objective, asset allocation pattern, investment strategy, risk factors, benchmark, fund manager, loads, minimum investment and plans and options. It is the main document for judging whether a scheme fits an investor. It is updated at least once a year.

points.heading: Statement of Additional Information
points.text: The SAI holds information common to all schemes of the fund house: the sponsor, AMC, trustees, service providers, legal and tax information, and the AMC's general policies. It is incorporated into the SID by reference and updated periodically. One SAI serves every scheme of the fund.

points.heading: Key Information Memorandum
points.text: The KIM is a short summary of the SID and must accompany every application form. It gives the essential facts - objective, asset allocation, risk, expenses, loads and past performance - so investors can decide without reading the full SID.

points.heading: Riskometer
points.text: SEBI's riskometer has six levels: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High. It is computed from the portfolio's risk value and reviewed monthly, so a scheme's risk level can change. Benchmarks also carry a riskometer. Changes must be disclosed to unit holders.

points.heading: Fundamental attributes
points.text: Fundamental attributes are the type of scheme, investment objective, investment pattern and terms such as liquidity provisions and fees. Changing them needs trustees' and SEBI's approval, written communication to unit holders and an exit window without exit load. The exit window is typically at least 30 days.

points.heading: Plans and options
points.text: Every scheme has a direct plan (no distributor commission, lower expense ratio) and a regular plan. Options include Growth, where gains stay in the NAV, and IDCW (income distribution cum capital withdrawal), where payouts come out of the investor's own capital and gains.

points.heading: Periodic disclosures
points.text: Schemes disclose NAV daily on the AMC and AMFI websites, portfolios at least monthly or fortnightly as required, half-yearly financial results and an annual report. These let investors check that the portfolio matches the stated objective. Fund factsheets add monthly details such as expense ratio, portfolio turnover and fund manager names.

points.heading: New Fund Offer
points.text: An NFO is the first offer of a scheme's units. Most NFOs stay open for no more than 15 days (ELSS can differ). Units are allotted at the face value plus any applicable charges, and the scheme must reopen for continuous sale and repurchase within a few business days.

traps: Thinking the KIM replaces the SID legally - the KIM summarises, while the SID remains the detailed document.
Placing AMC and sponsor details in the SID; they are in the SAI.
Assuming the riskometer is fixed at launch; it is evaluated monthly and can move up or down.
Calling IDCW a bonus or extra income; it is paid out of the NAV, which falls by the payout amount.
items.recap: SID = scheme-specific facts; SAI = fund-house facts; KIM = summary that goes with every form. The riskometer has six levels, from Low to Very High, reviewed monthly. Changing a fundamental attribute needs approvals, notice and a load-free exit. Direct plans skip commission; IDCW payouts reduce NAV.

items.title: Mutual Fund Distribution Channels: NISM V-A Notes
items.description: ARN, EUIN, commissions, direct plans, channel types and due diligence: revise how mutual funds are sold in India for the NISM Series V-A exam.
items.intro: This chapter explains how mutual funds reach investors: the types of distributors, the registration process, how distributors are paid and the rules that protect investors from mis-selling. Questions frequently test ARN and EUIN, upfront versus trail commission, the direct plan and the role of stock exchange and online platforms.

points.heading: Distribution channels
points.text: Funds are sold by individual distributors, banks, national distributors, stock brokers, online platforms and directly by AMCs. Exchange platforms such as NSE's NMF II and BSE StAR MF let brokers process transactions; MF Central and MF Utility offer common transaction services.

points.heading: Becoming a distributor
points.text: An individual must pass NISM Series V-A, then obtain an AMFI Registration Number (ARN) through KYD (Know Your Distributor) formalities. Employees of corporate distributors who interact with investors need an Employee Unique Identification Number (EUIN). The ARN must be quoted on every application form so that commission is correctly tracked and paid.

points.heading: Validity and CPE
points.text: The NISM certificate is valid for three years. To renew, distributors either retake the exam or attend Continuing Professional Education (CPE) as specified. An expired ARN means the distributor cannot earn commission on new business. Distributors should track the expiry date of both the certificate and the ARN, since lapses interrupt trail commission on new investments.

points.heading: Commission structure
points.text: SEBI has banned upfront commission paid out of scheme expenses; distributors earn trail commission, a percentage of the assets they bring, paid as long as the investor remains invested. Commission is part of the regular plan's expense ratio. Trail is paid monthly or quarterly by the AMC.

points.heading: Commission disclosure
points.text: Distributors must disclose commissions received from competing schemes. The Consolidated Account Statement shows the commission paid to the distributor on the investor's holdings, helping investors see what they pay. This transparency lets investors compare the cost of using a distributor with investing directly in the scheme's direct plan.

points.heading: Direct plans
points.text: Every scheme has a direct plan for investors who invest without a distributor. Its expense ratio is lower because no commission is paid, so its NAV is typically higher than the regular plan's over time. Investors can buy direct plans through AMC websites, MF Central or RTA offices.

points.heading: Mutual Fund Distributor vs RIA
points.text: A distributor earns commission from AMCs and may give incidental advice. A SEBI-registered investment adviser charges fees to clients and cannot also earn commission on the same client. Distributors may not call themselves 'independent financial advisers'. Relatives and group entities are also checked for this separation of roles.

points.heading: Due diligence and churning
points.text: AMCs perform due diligence on large distributors. Churning - switching a client between schemes to earn more commission - and rebating commission to clients are prohibited. Distributors must sell only suitable products after assessing the client's needs. Every recommendation should be documented.

points.heading: Payment rules
points.text: Cheques must be drawn in favour of the scheme, not the distributor. Third-party payments are not accepted except limited cases such as a parent investing for a minor, an employer for employees or a custodian for an FPI. Such exceptions require prescribed declarations.

traps: Thinking distributors still earn upfront commission from scheme expenses - SEBI banned this; trail is the main mode.
Confusing ARN (for the distributor firm or individual) with EUIN (for an employee of a distributor).
Assuming a direct plan has a different portfolio; the portfolio is identical, only the expense ratio differs.
Writing cheques to the distributor's name - payments always go to the scheme.
items.recap: Pass NISM V-A, get an ARN from AMFI; employees need an EUIN. Certificates last three years; renew by exam or CPE. Distributors earn trail commission, shown in the CAS. Direct plans have no commission and a lower TER. No churning, no rebating, no third-party cheques except permitted cases.

items.chapter: NAV, TER and Pricing of Units
items.title: NAV, TER and Mutual Fund Unit Pricing: V-A Notes
items.description: Calculate NAV, understand total expense ratio, exit load, cut-off timings and the sale and repurchase price for the NISM V-A distributor exam.
items.intro: This numerical chapter covers how NAV is calculated, what expenses can be charged to a scheme, how loads affect the price an investor gets and which day's NAV applies to a transaction. Expect two or three calculation questions on NAV or exit load plus rule questions on cut-off times and valuation.

points.heading: NAV calculation
points.text: NAV per unit = (market value of investments + other assets + accrued income - liabilities - accrued expenses) / units outstanding. A scheme with assets of ₹120 crore, liabilities of ₹2 crore and 8 crore units has NAV of ₹14.75.

points.heading: Valuation principles
points.text: Securities are valued at market prices; thinly traded or non-traded securities follow SEBI's fair valuation norms, using prices from valuation agencies for debt. Accrued interest and dividends declared but not received count as income on an accrual basis. Valuation policies are approved by the AMC's board and the trustees.

points.heading: Total expense ratio
points.text: TER is the annual percentage of daily net assets charged for management fees, distribution, registrar, audit and marketing costs. SEBI caps TER in slabs that fall as AUM rises, with lower caps for debt and index schemes. TER limits are revised periodically - check current SEBI rules.

points.heading: Effect of TER on returns
points.text: TER is deducted daily from the scheme's assets, so NAV is already net of expenses. Two identical portfolios earning 12% gross with TERs of 0.5% and 1.5% deliver roughly 11.5% and 10.5% to investors. Over 20 years, that one-percentage-point gap can reduce the final corpus by roughly a fifth.

points.heading: Entry and exit loads
points.text: Entry load is banned since 2009. Exit load is charged when units are redeemed within a specified period - for example 1% if redeemed within one year. Exit load is credited back to the scheme, not kept by the AMC.

points.heading: Repurchase price
points.text: Repurchase price = NAV x (1 - exit load). With NAV of ₹50 and 1% exit load, the investor receives ₹49.50 per unit. Sale price for purchases equals the applicable NAV, as no entry load is allowed. Exit loads usually lapse after a stated period.

points.heading: Cut-off timings
points.text: For most schemes, applications received by 3 pm get the same day's NAV for redemptions. For purchases, NAV applies based on when funds are realised in the scheme's account, irrespective of amount. Liquid and overnight funds have a 1:30 pm cut-off for purchases and use the previous day's NAV.

points.heading: Stamp duty
points.text: A stamp duty of 0.005% applies on purchase of mutual fund units, including SIP instalments and switch-ins, reducing the units allotted slightly. Redemptions do not attract stamp duty. On a ₹1,00,000 purchase, it works out to ₹5, so the units allotted are calculated on ₹99,995 rather than the full amount.

points.heading: Swing pricing
points.text: Swing pricing adjusts NAV for certain debt schemes during large outflows so that exiting investors bear the cost of liquidating assets, protecting those who stay. It applies mainly in stressed market conditions. The swing factor and the conditions that trigger it are disclosed in the scheme documents.

formulas: NAV per unit = (Assets - Liabilities) / Units outstanding
Redemption amount = Units x NAV x (1 - exit load %)
Units allotted = (Amount - stamp duty) / Applicable NAV
traps: Thinking exit load goes to the AMC as income - it is credited to the scheme.
Believing a lower NAV means a 'cheaper' or better fund; NAV level says nothing about value.
Applying the 3 pm cut-off rule blindly to liquid fund purchases - their cut-off is 1:30 pm.
Forgetting that NAV is already net of TER; expenses are not deducted again from redemption proceeds.
items.recap: NAV = net assets / units. TER is charged daily and capped in slabs by SEBI. No entry load; exit load returns to the scheme. Repurchase price = NAV less exit load. Cut-offs: 3 pm generally, 1:30 pm for liquid and overnight purchases; purchase NAV depends on realisation of funds. Stamp duty of 0.005% applies on purchases.

items.title: Mutual Fund Taxation for NISM V-A: Revision Notes
items.description: Equity vs debt fund taxation, holding periods, LTCG and STCG, IDCW tax, TDS and STT for mutual funds, revised for the NISM V-A exam as of 2026.
items.intro: Taxation questions in V-A test the classification of schemes, holding periods for long-term status, how capital gains and IDCW are taxed, and STT. Tax rates change through Union Budgets, so understand the structure and check current rates with the income tax department. The figures below reflect rules as of 2026.

points.heading: Equity-oriented fund
points.text: For tax purposes an equity-oriented fund invests at least 65% of its assets in equity shares of domestic listed companies. Equity fund of funds can also qualify if they meet the specified thresholds. Arbitrage funds qualify because their hedged equity counts as equity.

points.heading: Equity fund capital gains
points.text: Units held for more than 12 months are long-term. As of 2026, LTCG above ₹1.25 lakh a year is taxed at 12.5% and STCG at 20%, following the July 2024 changes. Rates change through Budgets - check the latest Finance Act.

points.heading: Specified (debt) mutual funds
points.text: Funds with more than 65% in debt and money market instruments, bought on or after 1 April 2023, are taxed at the investor's slab rate regardless of holding period. There is no indexation benefit. Older investments follow transition rules. Holding period no longer matters for these.

points.heading: Other funds
points.text: Schemes that are neither equity-oriented nor specified debt funds - such as some gold ETFs, international funds and certain hybrids - have their own holding period (generally 24 months for unlisted units, 12 for listed) and rates. Questions usually test the concept rather than every case.

points.heading: IDCW taxation
points.text: Income distributed under IDCW is taxed in the investor's hands at slab rates. The fund deducts TDS for resident individuals above the threshold set in the Act (raised to ₹10,000 a year from April 2025). Growth option investors are taxed only when they redeem.

points.heading: Securities Transaction Tax
points.text: STT applies on redemption of equity-oriented fund units (paid by the seller) and on purchase or sale of equity ETF units on the exchange. Debt fund transactions do not attract STT. STT is a transaction levy and is separate from capital gains tax, which is computed on the gain itself.

points.heading: Set-off of losses
points.text: Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short-term and long-term gains; long-term losses only against long-term gains. Unabsorbed losses can be carried forward for eight years if the return is filed on time. Capital losses cannot be set off against salary income.

points.heading: ELSS and deduction
points.text: ELSS investments qualify for a deduction (up to ₹1.5 lakh with other eligible items) only under the old tax regime. Each SIP instalment has its own three-year lock-in. ELSS gains are taxed like any equity fund on redemption. The new regime offers no such deduction.

points.heading: Switches and SWP
points.text: A switch between schemes, or between plans of the same scheme, is a redemption plus a fresh purchase and triggers capital gains. Each SWP instalment is partly capital and partly gain, and only the gain portion is taxed. Exit loads may apply too.

formulas: Equity-oriented: at least 65% in domestic listed equity; long term after 12 months
Capital gain = Redemption value - Cost of acquisition (units x purchase NAV)
traps: Assuming all debt funds get long-term treatment after three years - specified debt funds bought after 1 April 2023 are always taxed at slab.
Thinking a switch within the same fund house is tax-free; it is a sale and purchase.
Forgetting each ELSS SIP instalment has its own three-year lock-in.
Quoting tax rates as permanent - rates change through Budgets, so learn the structure and check current rates.
items.recap: Equity-oriented = 65%+ domestic equity; long term after 12 months; LTCG beyond the annual exemption at a concessional rate (12.5% as of 2026). Debt funds bought after April 2023 are taxed at slab. IDCW is taxed at slab with TDS above a threshold. Switches are taxable. STT applies on equity fund redemptions.

items.title: Mutual Fund Investor Services: NISM V-A Revision
items.description: KYC, folio, SIP, STP, SWP, nomination, account statements, NRI and minor investments: revise mutual fund investor services for the NISM V-A exam.
items.intro: Investor Services is a large, practical chapter: how an investor opens a folio, completes KYC, transacts, and keeps records updated. It covers systematic plans, nomination, minors, NRIs and timelines for payments. Expect many scenario questions where you must pick the right service or the right document.

points.heading: KYC process
points.text: KYC is a one-time process recorded with a KYC Registration Agency (KRA). PAN is mandatory, along with proof of identity and address, and in-person or video verification. Aadhaar-based eKYC is allowed. Central KYC (CKYC) gives a KYC Identification Number usable across financial sectors.

points.heading: Micro investments
points.text: Investments up to ₹50,000 a year per investor per fund house (including SIPs) can be made without PAN using PAN-exempt KYC with another photo ID. These are often called micro SIPs. The limit is counted across all schemes of the same fund house, so the investor must track total yearly investments carefully.

points.heading: Folio and CAS
points.text: A folio number identifies an investor's account with an AMC; one folio can hold many schemes. A Consolidated Account Statement is sent monthly if there is a transaction (otherwise half-yearly) and covers holdings across fund houses linked to the PAN, including demat holdings.

points.heading: Systematic plans
points.text: SIP invests a fixed amount at regular intervals and benefits from rupee cost averaging. STP moves a fixed amount from one scheme (often liquid) to another of the same fund house. SWP pays out a fixed amount regularly from a scheme, useful for retirees.

points.heading: Rupee cost averaging
points.text: Investing ₹1,000 a month buys 100 units at NAV ₹10 and 125 at ₹8, giving an average cost of about ₹8.89 - lower than the simple average NAV of ₹9. SIPs do not guarantee profit; they smooth the purchase price.

points.heading: Nomination
points.text: Individuals holding singly or jointly can nominate persons, with percentage shares. Nomination or an explicit opt-out declaration is required for new folios. SEBI expanded nomination rules in 2025 - check the current maximum number of nominees. Nominees can be changed any time.

points.heading: Minors
points.text: A minor's folio is held by the minor as sole holder with a parent or court-appointed guardian. Payment must come from the minor's bank account or a joint account with the guardian. On turning 18, the status must change to major with fresh KYC, or transactions are frozen.

points.heading: NRIs and others
points.text: NRIs can invest on repatriable (NRE) or non-repatriable (NRO) basis; some AMCs restrict investors from the US and Canada due to FATCA. TDS applies on NRI redemptions. Companies, trusts and HUFs need their own documents such as board resolutions. NRIs must also update their overseas address.

points.heading: Service timelines
points.text: Redemption proceeds must be paid within three working days for most schemes (longer for some schemes with overseas exposure). IDCW must be paid within seven working days of the record date. Delays attract interest payable by the AMC. The interest rate for delay is 15% a year.

points.heading: Transmission and pledge
points.text: On death of a unit holder, units pass to the joint holder, then the nominee, then legal heirs through transmission with documents such as the death certificate. Units can also be pledged or marked with a lien for loans. Documents needed vary by claimant.

formulas: Average cost under SIP = Total amount invested / Total units bought
traps: Mixing STP and SWP: STP shifts money between schemes; SWP pays money to the investor.
Assuming rupee cost averaging guarantees gains - it only lowers average cost in fluctuating markets.
Thinking a nominee becomes legal owner in all cases; the nominee may hold units in trust for legal heirs.
Letting a minor's folio continue after 18 without changing status - transactions get frozen.
items.recap: KYC once via KRA; PAN mandatory except micro SIP up to ₹50,000 a year. Folio = account; CAS consolidates holdings by PAN. SIP buys, STP moves, SWP withdraws. Redemption within three working days; IDCW within seven. Minors hold singly with a guardian and must convert at 18. Nominate or opt out explicitly.

items.chapter: Risk, Return and Performance of Funds
items.title: Mutual Fund Risk and Return: NISM V-A Revision Notes
items.description: Drivers of equity and debt fund returns, risk measures like standard deviation, beta and duration, and return calculations for NISM V-A revision.
items.intro: This chapter explains where fund returns come from, which risks drive the ups and downs of equity, debt and hybrid funds, and how risk is measured. Questions combine concepts (what affects a gilt fund's NAV?) with simple calculations of absolute return, CAGR and the impact of interest rate changes.

points.heading: Sources of return
points.text: Returns come from income (dividends, interest) and capital gains or losses. In the growth option both stay in the NAV; under IDCW part is paid out. Total return accounts for both price change and payouts. Comparing NAVs alone misses IDCW payouts.

points.heading: Equity fund drivers
points.text: Equity NAVs move with company earnings, valuations (P/E multiples), economic growth, interest rates, liquidity flows and sentiment. Fundamental analysis studies a company's business and financials; technical analysis studies price and volume patterns. Over long periods, earnings growth explains most equity returns, while short-term moves are dominated by sentiment and flows.

points.heading: Growth and value styles
points.text: Growth investing buys companies with fast-rising earnings, often at high P/E. Value investing buys companies trading below estimated intrinsic value. Style matters because one style can underperform for years. Value funds often do well after market crashes, while growth funds tend to lead in strong bull phases; mixing styles smooths results.

points.heading: Debt fund drivers
points.text: Debt fund returns come from accrual (interest earned) and mark-to-market changes. When yields fall, bond prices and NAVs rise; when yields rise, NAVs fall. Longer duration means bigger price swings. When the RBI cuts the repo rate and yields fall, a long duration gilt fund can deliver a sharp short-term gain, and the reverse when rates rise.

points.heading: Modified duration
points.text: Modified duration estimates the percentage price change for a 1% change in yield. A fund with modified duration of 5 will lose about 5% if yields rise by 1% (100 basis points). Liquid funds have very low duration and therefore low interest rate risk.

points.heading: Credit risk
points.text: Lower-rated bonds pay higher yields but may default or be downgraded. A downgrade lowers the bond's price. Credit risk funds deliberately hold lower-rated papers; side-pocketing can separate a defaulted security from the main portfolio. Investors should check portfolio ratings in the monthly disclosure.

points.heading: Standard deviation
points.text: Standard deviation measures total volatility of returns around the average. A fund with an average return of 12% and standard deviation of 18% swings much more than one with 12% and 8%. It assumes returns are roughly normally distributed and treats upside and downside swings alike, which is why some analysts prefer downside measures.

points.heading: Beta
points.text: Beta measures sensitivity to the market. A beta of 1.2 means the fund tends to rise or fall about 12% when the market moves 10%. Beta captures only systematic risk, so it is meaningful for diversified portfolios. Low-beta funds suit cautious investors.

points.heading: Hybrid and other funds
points.text: Hybrid fund returns depend on the equity-debt mix. Gold funds follow international gold prices and the rupee-dollar rate. International funds add currency risk: a falling rupee boosts returns from overseas assets. An aggressive hybrid fund with 75% equity will behave much like an equity fund, while a conservative hybrid with 20% equity behaves more like a debt fund.

formulas: Absolute return = (Ending NAV - Beginning NAV) / Beginning NAV x 100
CAGR = (Ending value / Beginning value)^(1/years) - 1
Approx price change of bond fund = - Modified duration x change in yield
traps: Saying bond prices rise when interest rates rise - the relationship is inverse.
Using absolute return for periods longer than a year; compare long periods using CAGR.
Treating standard deviation and beta as the same - SD is total risk, beta is market-related risk.
Assuming liquid funds carry no risk at all; they have low but not zero credit and interest rate risk.
items.recap: Returns = income + capital gain. Equity NAVs follow earnings and valuations; debt NAVs move inversely to yields, more so for longer duration. Modified duration x yield change approximates the price change. Credit risk rises as ratings fall. SD measures total volatility, beta measures market sensitivity. Use CAGR beyond one year.

items.title: Mutual Fund Scheme Performance and Benchmarks: V-A Notes
items.description: Benchmarks, TRI, tracking error, Sharpe and Treynor ratios, SIP returns and peer comparison: revise scheme performance evaluation for NISM V-A.
items.intro: Once a scheme has a track record, investors need to judge it against a benchmark and peers. This chapter covers benchmark selection, the Total Return Index, risk-adjusted measures and how returns are presented. Questions test which measure to use in which situation and include short calculations of Sharpe ratio or tracking error concepts.

points.heading: Purpose of a benchmark
points.text: A benchmark shows what a passive investment in the same market segment would have earned. A large cap fund is compared with an index such as Nifty 100 or BSE 100, not with a small cap index or a bank FD.

points.heading: Total Return Index
points.text: SEBI requires schemes to benchmark against the Total Return Index (TRI), which assumes dividends are reinvested. Comparing a fund with a price-only index flatters the fund because the index ignores dividends. A price index may lag the TRI by 1-1.5% a year because it ignores dividends paid by constituent companies.

points.heading: Tiered benchmarks
points.text: SEBI introduced a two-tier benchmark structure: the first tier reflects the category (common for all funds in that category), and an optional second tier reflects the fund's own style. This makes comparisons across fund houses fairer. Both tiers must be disclosed in documents.

points.heading: Peer comparison
points.text: Funds should be compared with others in the same SEBI category. Comparing a liquid fund's return with a small cap fund's is meaningless because their objectives and risks differ completely. Even within equity, a mid cap fund should be compared with mid cap peers and a mid cap index, not with large cap funds or the Nifty 50.

points.heading: Sharpe ratio
points.text: Sharpe = (fund return - risk-free rate) / standard deviation. A fund returning 14% with SD 16% and risk-free rate 6% has a Sharpe ratio of 0.5. Higher is better; it rewards return per unit of total risk. It suits concentrated or partly diversified funds.

points.heading: Treynor ratio and alpha
points.text: Treynor = (fund return - risk-free rate) / beta, suitable for diversified portfolios. Alpha is the excess return over what the fund's beta would predict; positive alpha signals manager skill, at least for that period. Alpha from one year can be luck rather than skill.

points.heading: Tracking error
points.text: Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between a fund's return and its benchmark's. Index funds and ETFs aim to minimise it; causes include expenses, cash holdings and delays in rebalancing. A tracking error of 0.1% is excellent for an index fund; 1% would suggest poor replication or high costs relative to peers.

points.heading: SIP returns and rolling returns
points.text: SIP returns are computed with XIRR because each instalment is invested at a different date. Rolling returns show performance over many overlapping periods, revealing consistency better than a single point-to-point figure. For example, three-year rolling returns calculated daily over ten years show how often a fund beat its benchmark, not just whether it did so once.

formulas: Sharpe = (Rp - Rf) / Standard deviation
Treynor = (Rp - Rf) / Beta
Jensen's alpha = Rp - [Rf + Beta x (Rm - Rf)]
traps: Comparing a fund with a price-return index instead of the TRI, which overstates outperformance.
Using Treynor for a concentrated, undiversified fund - Sharpe is the better measure there.
Assuming a fund with the highest one-year return is the best; check consistency and risk-adjusted returns.
Confusing tracking error (volatility of the difference) with simply the return gap in one year.
items.recap: Benchmark = what passive investing in the same segment earned; use TRI. Compare within the SEBI category. Sharpe uses SD, Treynor uses beta, alpha measures excess over beta-predicted return. Tracking error matters for index funds. Use XIRR for SIPs and rolling returns for consistency.

items.title: How to Select a Mutual Fund Scheme: NISM V-A Notes
items.description: Matching schemes to goals, risk profile and horizon, choosing category, plan and option, and avoiding selection mistakes - NISM V-A revision notes.
items.intro: The final chapter brings everything together: how a distributor helps an investor choose a category, a scheme within it, and the right plan and option. Questions are scenario-based - an investor's age, goal and risk appetite are described and you must pick a suitable product or reject an unsuitable one.

points.heading: Start with the investor
points.text: Selection begins with risk profiling: age, income stability, dependants, existing assets, investment horizon and comfort with losses. Suitability is the distributor's duty; an unsuitable sale is mis-selling even if the product is good. The profile should be recorded and refreshed when life events such as marriage, a child or retirement change the investor's situation.

points.heading: Match horizon to category
points.text: Money needed within months suits overnight, liquid or money market funds. A three-to-five-year goal may suit short duration debt or conservative hybrid funds. Goals seven or more years away can carry meaningful equity exposure. Equity needs time to recover from falls, which is why short-term money should not be parked in equity funds however attractive recent returns look.

points.heading: Asset allocation first
points.text: Decide the equity-debt-gold mix before picking schemes. For a 30-year-old saving for retirement, a high equity share is reasonable; for a 62-year-old needing monthly income, mostly debt with some equity for inflation protection is more typical. Studies of portfolios show allocation explains far more of the variation in outcomes than scheme choice.

points.heading: Selecting within a category
points.text: Compare schemes on consistency of rolling returns, risk-adjusted measures, expense ratio, portfolio quality, fund manager tenure and AUM. For debt funds, check average maturity, duration and credit quality of holdings. A scheme with steady second-quartile performance across market cycles is often a better choice than one that alternates between top and bottom.

points.heading: Active or passive
points.text: In segments where active managers struggle to beat the index after costs, such as large caps, low-cost index funds are a strong option. Active funds may add value in less efficient segments, but there is no assurance. Cost differences compound strongly over long horizons.

points.heading: Plan and option choice
points.text: Direct plans suit investors who can choose and monitor schemes themselves. Regular plans include the distributor's service cost. The growth option suits long-term wealth building; IDCW suits those wanting periodic cash, bearing in mind payouts are not assured. IDCW payouts are taxed at slab rates, so growth plus SWP may be more tax-efficient for some investors.

points.heading: Avoid common errors
points.text: Chasing last year's top performer, holding too many overlapping schemes, ignoring exit loads and taxes on switching, and stopping SIPs during market falls all hurt outcomes. Review the portfolio at least annually and rebalance. Distributors add the most value by keeping investors disciplined through volatile periods rather than by picking star funds.

points.heading: Model portfolios
points.text: Distributors often build model portfolios by life stage - for example, aggressive for young earners, moderate for mid-career families and conservative for retirees. These are starting points and must be customised to the individual. Two investors of the same age may need very different portfolios if one has stable government employment and the other runs a seasonal business.

traps: Recommending a sectoral or small cap fund to a retiree needing capital safety because it 'performed best' recently.
Selecting a scheme before deciding the asset allocation - allocation drives most of the portfolio's risk and return.
Assuming IDCW payouts are regular income guaranteed by the fund; they depend on distributable surplus.
Owning several schemes of the same category, which adds overlap rather than diversification.
items.recap: Profile the investor, then set asset allocation, then pick the category, then the scheme, then plan and option. Short horizons need liquid or short debt; long horizons can hold equity. Judge schemes on consistency, risk-adjusted returns, costs and portfolio quality. Avoid chasing past winners and review annually.

items.title: NISM V-B Investment Landscape: Revision Notes
items.description: Inflation, compounding, liquidity, asset classes and matching investments to goals - beginner-friendly revision notes for the NISM V-B foundation exam.
items.intro: V-B is written for first-time distributors, so this chapter keeps the basics simple: why money left idle loses value, how compounding builds wealth, and how common asset classes differ in risk, return and liquidity. Expect small calculations with round numbers and situational questions such as which asset suits a young saver or a retiree.

points.heading: Why idle money shrinks
points.text: If a family keeps ₹1 lakh in a cupboard and prices rise 6% a year, after one year that cash buys what ₹94,000 or so bought earlier. Inflation quietly reduces purchasing power, which is why the workbook argues that savings need to be invested, not just stored.

points.heading: Saving vs investing
points.text: Saving means not spending part of income. Investing means putting those savings into assets expected to earn a return - interest, dividends or price growth. A recurring deposit, a PPF account and an equity SIP are all investments, though with very different risk levels.

points.heading: Compounding at work
points.text: Compounding means earning returns on earlier returns. ₹1,00,000 at 10% a year becomes ₹1,10,000 after one year and ₹1,21,000 after two, because the second year's interest is earned on ₹1,10,000. Starting early matters more than investing large amounts later. Ten years at 10% roughly multiplies money 2.6 times.

points.heading: Common asset classes
points.text: Cash and bank deposits are safe and liquid but earn modestly. Debt (bonds, deposits) offers steadier income. Equity offers the highest long-run growth with sharp short-term swings. Gold acts as a hedge in crises. Real estate needs large sums and is hard to sell quickly.

points.heading: Liquidity
points.text: Liquidity is how quickly an investment can be converted to cash at a fair value. A savings account is instantly liquid; an open-ended mutual fund pays within a few working days; a plot of land might take months to sell and may need a discount.

points.heading: Risk and return trade-off
points.text: Higher expected return comes with higher risk. A bank FD gives predictable interest; an equity fund can gain 25% in one year and fall 20% the next. No product offers high returns with no risk, and claims of that kind are a warning sign.

points.heading: Types of risk
points.text: Inflation risk erodes purchasing power. Market risk affects all shares together. Credit risk is the borrower failing to pay. Liquidity risk is being unable to sell. Concentration risk comes from putting too much into one company or sector, which diversification addresses.

points.heading: Goals and time horizon
points.text: A goal needs an amount and a date. Money needed in six months for a wedding should stay in safe, liquid options; a retirement 35 years away can be built mostly with equity. A 25-year-old with stable income can usually accept more risk than a 60-year-old.

points.heading: Diversification
points.text: Spreading money across many companies and sectors reduces the damage if one company fails. A mutual fund holding 50 stocks protects the investor far better than owning two or three shares directly, though it cannot avoid a fall in the whole market.

formulas: Value after n years = Amount x (1 + r)^n
Real return is roughly the interest rate minus the inflation rate
traps: Assuming money in a savings account is 'safe' from loss - its purchasing power can fall when inflation exceeds the interest rate.
Confusing liquidity with safety: a listed small company share is easy to sell but risky.
Thinking diversification removes all risk; it reduces company-specific risk but not market-wide falls.
Using simple interest when the question says compounded annually - interest is added to the principal each year.
items.recap: Inflation shrinks idle money, so invest. Compounding rewards starting early. Cash and deposits are safe, debt is steady, equity grows most but swings most, gold hedges crises, property is illiquid. Match the product to the goal's date. Diversify across companies and sectors to cut concentration risk.

items.chapter: Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund
items.title: Mutual Fund Basics for NISM V-B: Revision Notes
items.description: What a mutual fund is, how units and NAV work, open vs closed-ended schemes and SEBI equity categories - simple revision notes for the NISM V-B exam.
items.intro: This chapter answers the question every new investor asks: what exactly is a mutual fund and why should I use one? It covers pooling, units, NAV, the main scheme structures and SEBI's categories for equity, debt and hybrid funds. Questions are direct definitions plus scenarios about exiting closed-ended schemes and identifying fund categories.

points.heading: Pooling explained
points.text: Imagine 10,000 people each contributing ₹5,000. The ₹5 crore pool is invested by a professional fund manager across many securities. Each person receives units in proportion to the money contributed, so all investors share gains and losses in the same proportion. Unit holders are owners, not lenders.

points.heading: Benefits
points.text: Small ticket sizes (SIPs from a few hundred rupees), professional management, instant diversification, easy liquidity in open-ended schemes, regular disclosures and SEBI regulation make funds attractive for small investors who cannot research and track dozens of shares themselves. Daily NAVs also make tracking easy.

points.heading: Open-ended schemes
points.text: Open-ended schemes buy and sell units every business day at NAV-based prices, so the number of units keeps changing. There is no maturity date. Most retail investments - SIPs in equity funds, liquid funds for parking cash - are in open-ended schemes.

points.heading: Closed-ended and interval schemes
points.text: A closed-ended scheme raises money only during its NFO and has a fixed maturity. Before maturity, investors exit by selling units on the stock exchange, where the price may be below NAV. Interval schemes allow transactions only during pre-set windows.

points.heading: Equity fund categories
points.text: SEBI defines large caps as the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation, mid caps as 101st to 250th and small caps as 251st onwards. Large cap funds keep at least 80% in large caps; mid cap and small cap funds at least 65% in their respective segments.

points.heading: Flexi cap and multi cap
points.text: A flexi cap fund must hold at least 65% in equity but can move freely across large, mid and small caps. A multi cap fund must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps, so it always carries meaningful small cap exposure.

points.heading: Debt and hybrid categories
points.text: Debt funds range from overnight and liquid funds for very short periods to gilt and long duration funds for rate-sensitive investors. Hybrid funds mix equity and debt; arbitrage funds earn the price gap between cash and futures markets, so their returns resemble low-risk debt funds.

points.heading: What funds cannot do
points.text: A mutual fund cannot assure returns on market-linked schemes, cannot prevent NAV falls, and investors have no say in which stocks are bought. Expenses are charged every day through the expense ratio, whether the fund gains or loses. Investors bear these costs in every market.

traps: Thinking a closed-ended scheme's units can be redeemed with the AMC anytime - before maturity, the exit is via the stock exchange.
Swapping the definitions of flexi cap (no segment minimum) and multi cap (25% each in large, mid and small).
Calling arbitrage funds high-risk equity funds; their hedged positions make returns closer to short-term debt.
Believing mutual fund investors are lenders who will get their principal back - they own units and bear losses.
items.recap: A fund pools money and issues units; investors share gains and losses proportionally. Open-ended = daily transactions; closed-ended = exit via exchange. Large cap = top 100, mid = 101-250, small = 251+. Large cap fund 80% in large caps; flexi cap 65% equity anywhere; multi cap 25% each. No returns are assured.

items.title: Mutual Fund Structure for NISM V-B: Sponsor to RTA
items.description: Revise the roles of sponsor, trustees, AMC, custodian and registrar, plus AMC net worth and why investor money stays safe, for the NISM V-B exam.
items.intro: New distributors must be able to explain who is behind a mutual fund and how investor money is protected. This chapter covers the trust structure and the job of each constituent. Questions typically describe a role - 'processes transactions', 'holds securities', 'oversees the AMC' - and ask which entity performs it.

points.heading: A fund is a trust
points.text: Every Indian mutual fund is set up as a trust. The sponsor creates it through a trust deed, and the assets of all schemes are held for the benefit of unit holders. This means the money belongs to investors, not to the company that runs the fund.

points.heading: Sponsor
points.text: The sponsor is the promoter - often a bank, financial group or insurer. It sets up the trust, appoints the trustees, and forms the asset management company, contributing to its capital. SEBI checks the sponsor's track record and financial strength before granting registration.

points.heading: Trustees
points.text: Trustees act as guardians of unit holders' interests. They approve new schemes, review the AMC's activities and compliance, and report to SEBI. At least two-thirds of trustees must be independent of the sponsor so that oversight is genuine. They can also remove the AMC if needed.

points.heading: Asset Management Company
points.text: The AMC is the professional manager. Its fund managers decide what to buy and sell; its teams handle research, operations, compliance and sales. SEBI requires an AMC to maintain net worth of at least ₹50 crore. The AMC earns a management fee as part of the scheme's expenses.

points.heading: Custodian
points.text: The custodian keeps the scheme's securities safe, settles purchases and sales, and collects dividends and interest. Separating custody from the AMC means the fund manager cannot simply take securities away; they sit with an independent, SEBI-registered entity. It also tracks bonus and rights issues.

points.heading: Registrar and Transfer Agent
points.text: The RTA is the investor's service desk. It processes purchases, redemptions, switches, KYC updates and address or bank changes, and sends account statements. In India, large RTAs serve many fund houses, which helps the consolidated statement system. CAMS and KFintech are the major RTAs.

points.heading: Supporting entities
points.text: Auditors check scheme accounts; fund accountants calculate NAV; bankers collect and pay money; distributors bring in investors. AMFI, the industry association, registers distributors and runs investor awareness, but it is not the regulator - SEBI is. The AMC remains responsible for outsourced work.

points.heading: Why investors are protected
points.text: Because scheme assets are owned by the trust and held by a custodian, they are not available to creditors of the sponsor or AMC. If an AMC is in trouble, the trustees can transfer management to another AMC, and investors' units continue to represent the same assets.

traps: Saying the AMC owns the scheme's assets; the trust owns them for unit holders and the custodian holds them.
Assigning portfolio management to trustees - trustees oversee; the AMC's fund managers manage.
Mixing up the custodian (holds securities) with the RTA (keeps investor records and processes transactions).
Forgetting that the minimum AMC net worth is ₹50 crore under current SEBI rules.
items.recap: Sponsor sets up the trust and AMC; trustees protect investors and supervise; AMC (₹50 crore net worth) manages money; custodian holds securities; RTA services investors. Assets belong to the trust, so investors are protected even if the AMC or sponsor faces trouble. SEBI regulates; AMFI is the industry body.

items.chapter: Mutual Fund Products for New Cadre Distributors
items.title: Mutual Fund Products for New Cadre Distributors: Notes
items.description: Index funds, ETFs, diversified equity, ELSS and simple debt funds that new cadre distributors sell - features, risks and suitability for NISM V-B.
items.intro: This chapter is unique to V-B. New cadre distributors may sell only a defined list of simple schemes, so the exam tests those products in detail: how index funds and ETFs work, why diversified equity is safer than sectoral funds, ELSS lock-in rules and basic debt options. Many questions describe an investor and ask which product suits them.

points.heading: Who is a new cadre distributor
points.text: The simplified 'new cadre' category was created to widen distribution to smaller towns. Individuals such as retired government and bank officials, teachers and postal agents can qualify by passing NISM V-B and obtaining an ARN. They can distribute only the simple schemes on AMFI's eligible list - check AMFI for the current list.

points.heading: Index funds
points.text: An index fund buys the stocks of an index, such as the Nifty 50, in the same proportions. It does not try to beat the index, only to track it. Costs are low because there is no stock research, and the risk of the fund manager picking wrong stocks is removed.

points.heading: Exchange Traded Funds
points.text: ETFs also track an index but are listed on a stock exchange. Investors buy and sell them through a broker during market hours at market prices close to the indicative NAV, and need a demat and trading account. Market makers help keep the price close to NAV.

points.heading: Tracking error
points.text: Passive funds do not match their index exactly because of expenses, cash held for redemptions and the time taken to rebalance. The variability of this gap is tracking error. Lower tracking error indicates better replication - an important comparison point between two index funds on the same index.

points.heading: Diversified equity funds
points.text: Large cap, flexi cap and similar diversified funds spread money across many sectors. If banking shares fall, holdings in FMCG, IT or pharma cushion the impact. A sectoral fund that holds only banking shares would take the full hit, which is why diversified funds are considered less risky.

points.heading: ELSS
points.text: Equity Linked Savings Schemes invest at least 80% in equity and carry a three-year lock-in. Under the old tax regime, investments qualify for a deduction within the overall limit for eligible savings. Each SIP instalment is locked in for three years from its own date: units bought in July 2024 become free in July 2027.

points.heading: Gold ETFs and gold funds
points.text: A gold ETF invests in physical gold of standard purity and trades on the exchange, so investors avoid storage, purity worries and making charges on jewellery. A gold fund of funds invests in gold ETFs and lets investors use SIPs without a demat account.

points.heading: Simple debt options
points.text: Overnight funds invest in one-day securities and liquid funds in instruments up to 91 days. They suit investors parking money for days or weeks, such as a business keeping cash for monthly salaries. Their returns track short-term interest rates and are not assured.

points.heading: Matching product to investor
points.text: A young salaried saver wanting low-cost long-term equity exposure fits an index fund SIP; a taxpayer under the old regime wanting a deduction may consider ELSS; someone parking a bonus for two months suits a liquid fund. Sectoral or thematic funds are not suitable for first-time, risk-averse investors.

formulas: Tracking difference = Fund return - Index return (tracking error is the standard deviation of this difference over time)
traps: Thinking an index fund aims to beat the index; it only tries to match it at low cost.
Believing ETF units are bought from the AMC at end-of-day NAV like ordinary funds - retail investors trade them on the exchange during market hours.
Assuming an ELSS SIP's whole investment unlocks three years after the first instalment; each instalment has its own lock-in.
Calling a sectoral fund 'diversified' just because it holds 30 stocks - all are in one sector.
items.recap: New cadre distributors sell only simple schemes on AMFI's list. Index funds and ETFs track an index at low cost; ETFs trade on exchanges and need demat. Tracking error measures how closely they follow. Diversified equity beats sectoral funds on risk. ELSS: 80% equity, three-year lock-in per instalment. Liquid and overnight funds park short-term cash.

items.title: Scheme Documents and Riskometer: NISM V-B Notes
items.description: SID, SAI, KIM, riskometer levels, factsheets and portfolio disclosure - where investors find scheme information, revised simply for NISM V-B.
items.intro: Before recommending any scheme, a distributor must know where its facts are published. This short chapter covers the offer documents, the riskometer and the regular disclosures fund houses make. Exam questions describe a piece of information and ask where it appears, or ask about riskometer levels.

points.heading: Scheme Information Document
points.text: The SID is the scheme's rulebook. It states the investment objective, asset allocation pattern, strategy, risk factors, benchmark, fund manager, loads, minimum amounts and available plans and options. A distributor checking whether a scheme can invest in overseas shares or lower-rated bonds would look here.

points.heading: Statement of Additional Information
points.text: The SAI covers the whole mutual fund rather than one scheme: details of the sponsor, AMC, trustees, custodian and other service providers, general tax information and investor rights. It is common to all schemes of that fund house and is read along with the SID.

points.heading: Key Information Memorandum
points.text: The KIM is a short version of the SID that must be attached to every application form. It shows the objective, asset allocation, risk level, expense ratio, loads, past performance and minimum investment, giving investors the essentials in a few pages.

points.heading: Riskometer levels
points.text: SEBI's riskometer shows a scheme's risk on six levels: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High. Most equity funds sit at Very High; overnight funds are usually Low. The rating is reviewed monthly based on the actual portfolio and can change.

points.heading: Benchmark riskometer
points.text: Scheme documents and factsheets also show the riskometer of the scheme's benchmark. Seeing both lets an investor judge whether the fund is taking more or less risk than its benchmark index. A large cap fund rated Very High alongside a benchmark also rated Very High is behaving as expected for its category.

points.heading: Portfolio disclosure
points.text: Funds publish their full portfolios at regular intervals on their own and AMFI's websites. This helps investors check that a scheme sticks to its stated style - for example, that a large cap fund is not quietly loading up on small caps.

points.heading: Factsheets and annual reports
points.text: Monthly factsheets summarise NAV, AUM, expense ratio, top holdings, sector allocation and returns versus benchmark. Annual reports or abridged summaries give audited accounts. Distributors use factsheets for quick reviews with clients. Distributors should always use the latest factsheet, since holdings and expense ratios change from month to month.

points.heading: Changes to a scheme
points.text: If an AMC wants to change a scheme's fundamental attributes - its type, objective or asset allocation - unit holders must be informed and given an exit option without exit load before the change takes effect. Merging two schemes is a common trigger for this.

traps: Looking for the AMC's board or sponsor details in the SID; they are in the SAI.
Assuming a scheme's riskometer is fixed for life; it is reviewed monthly.
Thinking the KIM is optional reading material; it must accompany every application form.
Forgetting that changes to fundamental attributes give investors a load-free exit window.
items.recap: SID = one scheme's details; SAI = fund-house-level details; KIM = summary attached to forms. Riskometer has six levels from Low to Very High and is reviewed monthly; benchmarks show one too. Portfolios and factsheets are published regularly. Fundamental changes need notice and a load-free exit.

items.title: New Cadre Distributor Rules: ARN, Commission, Conduct
items.description: How new cadre distributors register, earn trail commission and follow AMFI's code of conduct, including payment rules and suitability, for NISM V-B.
items.intro: This chapter explains how a new cadre distributor starts and runs the business: certification, registration, how commission works, what must be disclosed and how to avoid mis-selling. Questions are practical - whom the cheque should be drawn to, where commission appears, or why a recommendation is unsuitable.

points.heading: Getting started
points.text: To sell mutual funds and earn commission, an individual must pass the relevant NISM certification and register with AMFI to obtain an ARN. KYD (Know Your Distributor) verification is part of this. Employees of distribution firms who deal with investors need their own EUIN.

points.heading: Renewal
points.text: The NISM certificate is valid for three years. Distributors must renew it through CPE or by passing the exam again, and keep the ARN valid; otherwise they cannot earn commission on new investments. A new cadre distributor can later upgrade by passing NISM V-A to sell the full range.

points.heading: Trail commission
points.text: Distributors are paid trail commission, a small percentage of the investor's holding value, for as long as the money stays invested. Upfront commission out of scheme expenses is not allowed. This links the distributor's income to keeping clients invested and satisfied over years.

points.heading: Commission disclosure
points.text: Investors can see the commission paid to their distributor on their holdings in the Consolidated Account Statement. Distributors must disclose commissions from the different schemes they recommend so the investor can judge any conflict of interest. This helps investors weigh the cost of advice and service.

points.heading: Direct plan option
points.text: Every scheme has a direct plan with no distributor commission and therefore a lower expense ratio. Investors who prefer the distributor's guidance and service choose the regular plan, which includes the commission cost. Both plans hold exactly the same portfolio, so the direct plan's NAV gradually becomes higher than the regular plan's.

points.heading: Suitability
points.text: Recommending a small cap fund to a risk-averse retiree because it gave high recent returns is mis-selling. A distributor must understand the client's age, income, goals and risk tolerance, and recommend only products that fit. Past returns should never be presented as a promise.

points.heading: Payment rules
points.text: Investment cheques and online payments must be in favour of the scheme, never the distributor. Third-party payments are generally not accepted, with limited exceptions such as parents investing for a minor child. Cash investments are allowed only up to a small annual limit per investor.

points.heading: Prohibited practices
points.text: Distributors must not rebate commission to attract clients, churn investors between schemes, give false information about schemes or forge signatures. AMCs can stop commission and AMFI can suspend or cancel the ARN for breaches. Such misconduct also damages trust in the industry as a whole.

traps: Thinking a cheque can be written to the distributor's firm for convenience - it must be in favour of the scheme.
Believing upfront commission from scheme expenses is still paid; trail commission is the norm.
Assuming the direct plan has a different portfolio from the regular plan; only the expense ratio differs.
Treating a new cadre ARN as permission to sell every type of scheme.
items.recap: Pass NISM, get an ARN (employees need EUIN), renew every three years. Earn trail commission, visible to clients in the CAS. Direct plans carry no commission. Recommend only suitable products; never promise returns. Payments go to the scheme; no rebating or churning.

items.title: Mutual Fund Performance and Returns: NISM V-B Notes
items.description: Calculate absolute and total return, understand benchmarks, expense ratio impact and fair comparisons of mutual fund performance for NISM V-B revision.
items.intro: This chapter teaches distributors how to read and explain a fund's performance honestly. It covers simple return calculations, the role of benchmarks, why costs matter and how to compare like with like. Expect two or three easy calculations with round numbers, plus questions on choosing the right comparison.

points.heading: Absolute return
points.text: Absolute return is the simple percentage change in NAV. If a growth option NAV rises from ₹20 to ₹23, the return is (23 - 20) / 20 = 15%. It suits periods of up to one year; longer periods should be compared using annualised returns.

points.heading: Total return with IDCW
points.text: When a fund pays IDCW, the payout must be added back. A unit bought at ₹10, worth ₹12 after a year, which also paid ₹1 IDCW, earned (12 - 10 + 1) / 10 = 30%. Looking only at NAV would understate the return at 20%.

points.heading: Annualised return (CAGR)
