points.text: CAGR shows the steady yearly rate that turns the starting value into the ending value. ₹10,000 growing to ₹16,105 in five years is a CAGR of about 10%. CAGR hides the ups and downs along the way, so volatility should also be considered.

points.heading: Benchmarks
points.text: A benchmark is the yardstick for a fund's performance - usually an index that represents the fund's investment universe. A large cap fund that returned 14% when its benchmark returned 16% has underperformed, even though 14% looks attractive in isolation.

points.heading: Compare like with like
points.text: A liquid fund and a small cap fund have completely different objectives and risks, so comparing their returns is meaningless. Compare a scheme with its benchmark and with other schemes in the same SEBI category over the same period. Peer rankings are published by AMFI and data providers.

points.heading: Expense ratio matters
points.text: The TER is deducted from scheme assets daily. Two schemes earning 12% on identical portfolios, one with TER 0.5% and the other 1.5%, will give investors roughly 11.5% and 10.5%. Over 15 to 20 years the gap compounds into a large difference.

points.heading: Drivers of returns
points.text: Equity fund returns depend on company earnings, valuations and market mood; debt fund returns depend on interest income and changes in interest rates - bond prices fall when rates rise. Gold funds follow gold prices and the rupee. So the same news can affect equity and debt funds differently.

points.heading: Past performance caution
points.text: Scheme documents carry the warning that past performance may or may not be sustained. Distributors should present returns over several periods, alongside the benchmark, and never use one great year to sell a scheme. Returns over one, three and five years, shown together, give a fairer picture of a scheme's consistency.

formulas: Absolute return = (End NAV - Start NAV) / Start NAV x 100
Total return = (End NAV - Start NAV + IDCW received) / Start NAV x 100
CAGR = (End value / Start value)^(1/years) - 1
traps: Ignoring IDCW payouts when calculating return - add them back to get total return.
Quoting absolute return for a five-year period as if it were yearly; annualise it with CAGR.
Comparing a fund with a benchmark from a different segment, such as a mid cap fund against the Nifty 50.
Assuming a fund with a lower NAV is cheaper and therefore better value.
items.recap: Absolute return for up to a year, CAGR beyond. Add back IDCW for total return. Judge a fund against its benchmark and its category peers, not other categories. Lower expense ratio means more return for the investor. Past performance is not a promise.

items.title: Mutual Fund Tax Basics for NISM V-B Revision
items.description: Equity-oriented fund definition, holding periods, capital gains, IDCW tax, STT and ELSS deduction basics for NISM V-B, with rates as of 2026.
items.intro: Distributors are not tax advisers, but they must explain the basic tax treatment of the products they sell. V-B tests the equity-oriented definition, the holding period for long-term status, how IDCW is taxed and what STT is. Rates change with Budgets; rates below are as of 2026 and should be checked with the income tax department.

points.heading: Equity-oriented fund
points.text: A scheme is equity-oriented for tax purposes if at least 65% of its assets are in equity shares of domestic listed companies. Most diversified equity funds, index funds on Indian indices, ELSS and arbitrage funds qualify, which gives them concessional capital gains treatment.

points.heading: Holding period
points.text: Units of an equity-oriented fund become long-term capital assets when held for more than 12 months. Sell within 12 months and the gain is short-term. Holding periods are counted separately for each purchase, including every SIP instalment. Selling the oldest units first applies (first in, first out).

points.heading: Capital gains rates
points.text: As of 2026, long-term gains on equity-oriented funds above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year are taxed at 12.5%, while short-term gains are taxed at 20%. Debt-heavy funds bought after 1 April 2023 are taxed at the investor's slab rate. Check the current Finance Act before quoting rates.

points.heading: Growth vs IDCW
points.text: Under the growth option, tax arises only when units are sold. IDCW payouts are added to the investor's income and taxed at slab rates in the year received, with TDS above a threshold. A high-bracket investor may pay more tax under IDCW.

points.heading: Securities Transaction Tax
points.text: STT is a small tax charged on the sale (redemption) of equity-oriented fund units and on trades in equity ETFs on exchanges. It is collected automatically and is separate from capital gains tax. Debt fund redemptions do not attract STT.

points.heading: ELSS tax benefit
points.text: ELSS investments qualify for a deduction within the overall limit for eligible investments, but only for taxpayers who choose the old tax regime. Under the new regime there is no deduction, though ELSS remains a regular equity fund with a three-year lock-in.

points.heading: Switches are sales
points.text: Switching from one scheme to another, or from a regular plan to a direct plan of the same scheme, is treated as redeeming the old units and buying new ones. Capital gains tax and exit load can apply. Distributors should point this out before suggesting any switch.

points.heading: Stamp duty
points.text: A stamp duty of 0.005% is charged on purchases of mutual fund units, including each SIP instalment. It is not an income tax, but it slightly reduces the number of units allotted. On a ₹10,000 SIP instalment it amounts to just 50 paise, and redemptions are not charged.

traps: Assuming equity fund units become long-term after 36 months - for equity-oriented funds the period is 12 months.
Treating a switch within the same fund house as tax-free; it is a redemption and fresh purchase.
Believing IDCW is tax-free in the investor's hands - it is taxed at slab rates.
Quoting today's tax rates as fixed; they change through Budgets.
items.recap: Equity-oriented = at least 65% domestic equity; long-term after 12 months. LTCG above the annual exemption gets a concessional rate; STCG is higher. Debt funds bought after April 2023 are taxed at slab. IDCW is taxed at slab. STT applies on equity fund redemptions. ELSS deduction only in the old regime. Switches are taxable.

items.title: Mutual Fund Investor Services: NISM V-B Notes
items.description: KYC, folios, SIP, STP, SWP, switches, cut-off times and account statements explained for new cadre distributors preparing for the NISM V-B exam.
items.intro: New cadre distributors spend most of their time helping investors transact, so this chapter is heavily tested. It covers KYC, folios, systematic plans, cut-off timings and statements. Questions are short and practical: what document is mandatory, which plan moves money between schemes, which NAV applies.

points.heading: KYC requirements
points.text: Before investing, a resident individual must complete KYC once with a KYC Registration Agency. PAN is mandatory for regular investments, along with proof of address and in-person or video verification. Aadhaar-based eKYC speeds this up. Once done, KYC is valid across all fund houses.

points.heading: Folio number
points.text: A folio number is the investor's account number with a particular fund house. One folio can hold several schemes of that AMC. Quoting the existing folio on new applications keeps all investments together and avoids repeated paperwork. Investors can also consolidate folios.

points.heading: SIP
points.text: A Systematic Investment Plan invests a fixed amount at regular intervals - usually monthly - through an auto-debit mandate. Because more units are bought when NAV is low and fewer when it is high, the average cost per unit tends to be lower than the average NAV over the period.

points.heading: STP
points.text: A Systematic Transfer Plan moves a fixed amount at regular intervals from one scheme to another of the same fund house - commonly from a liquid fund to an equity fund. It suits someone with a lump sum who wants to enter equity gradually.

points.heading: SWP
points.text: A Systematic Withdrawal Plan lets an investor withdraw a fixed amount regularly from a scheme, for example ₹20,000 a month from a hybrid fund for a retiree's expenses. Each withdrawal redeems units, so the balance falls if returns are lower than withdrawals.

points.heading: Cut-off timings
points.text: For most schemes, redemption requests received before 3 pm get that day's NAV. For purchases, the NAV depends on when the money reaches the scheme's account. Liquid and overnight funds have a 1:30 pm cut-off for purchases. Liquid funds then apply the previous day's NAV.

points.heading: Switches
points.text: A switch redeems units in one scheme and buys units in another of the same fund house in a single instruction. It is treated as a redemption followed by a purchase, so exit load and capital gains tax may apply.

points.heading: Statements and timelines
points.text: Investors get a Consolidated Account Statement covering all their fund holdings by PAN. Redemption money is credited to the registered bank account within three working days for most schemes, and IDCW within seven working days of the record date. Delays attract interest payable by the AMC.

points.heading: Keeping records updated
points.text: Investors should update mobile number, email, bank account and nomination. Nomination, or a formal opt-out, is required. Changes of bank account need supporting documents, a safeguard against fraud. Outdated contact details are a common reason for missed communication and unclaimed redemption or IDCW amounts, which then sit with the fund house until claimed.

traps: Mixing STP (moves money between two schemes) with SWP (pays money out to the investor).
Thinking a switch is not a sale for tax; it is a redemption plus a purchase.
Assuming the folio number is the same across all AMCs - each fund house issues its own.
Applying the 3 pm purchase cut-off to liquid funds; theirs is 1:30 pm.
items.recap: KYC once via KRA, PAN mandatory. Folio = account with one AMC. SIP invests regularly, STP transfers between schemes, SWP withdraws. 3 pm cut-off (1:30 pm for liquid purchases). Switches are taxable redemptions. CAS consolidates holdings; redemptions paid within three working days.

items.title: Mutual Fund Regulation for NISM V-B: Revision Notes
items.description: SEBI's role, AMFI's code of ethics, investor rights, fundamental attribute changes and the complaint process for NISM V-B foundation exam revision.
items.intro: The last V-B chapter covers the rules that keep the industry honest: who regulates mutual funds, what AMFI does, what rights investors have and how complaints are resolved. Questions are straightforward but easy to mix up, especially the sequence of the complaint process and the difference between SEBI and AMFI.

points.heading: SEBI as regulator
points.text: Mutual funds in India are governed by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations framed under the SEBI Act, 1992. SEBI registers fund houses, approves the structure, sets rules on investments, expenses and disclosures, and can penalise AMCs, trustees and distributors. It also inspects AMCs periodically.

points.heading: AMFI's role
points.text: AMFI is the industry association of SEBI-registered AMCs. It registers distributors and issues ARNs, publishes the code of conduct for distributors and the AMFI Code of Ethics (ACE) for AMCs, runs investor awareness campaigns and publishes industry data. It is a self-regulatory body, not a statutory regulator.

points.heading: AMFI Code of Ethics
points.text: ACE sets standards of integrity, fairness, due diligence and disclosure for AMCs and their employees. It expects them to put investors' interests first, avoid misleading advertisements and maintain confidentiality of investor information. It covers advertising, record keeping and the handling of investor complaints as well, so that standards are consistent across fund houses.

points.heading: Distributor code of conduct
points.text: Distributors must act in the investor's interest, disclose commissions, provide scheme documents, recommend suitable schemes, avoid churning and never assure returns or misrepresent risk. Violations can lead to ARN suspension or cancellation. They must also keep KYD details current and maintain records of client interactions, so that recommendations can be reviewed if a complaint arises later.

points.heading: Investor rights
points.text: Unit holders own a proportionate share of scheme assets, receive statements and annual reports, can inspect key documents and are entitled to timely payment of redemptions and IDCW, with interest for delays. Delays in redemption or IDCW payments attract interest at 15% a year, paid by the AMC from its own resources, not from the scheme.

points.heading: Fundamental attribute changes
points.text: If an AMC proposes to change a fundamental attribute of a scheme, it needs trustee and SEBI approval, must inform unit holders in writing and must give them a window to exit at NAV without any exit load. The exit window is typically at least 30 days.

points.heading: Complaint process
points.text: An investor with a complaint, such as delayed redemption, should first approach the AMC or its RTA. If not satisfied, the investor can escalate to SEBI through the SCORES online portal, and thereafter use the SMART ODR platform for online conciliation or arbitration.

points.heading: Advertisements
points.text: Mutual fund advertisements must carry the standard warning that investments are subject to market risks and that investors should read scheme documents. Performance can be shown only in the format SEBI prescribes, alongside the benchmark. Promising or implying assured returns in an advertisement is prohibited.

traps: Calling AMFI the regulator of mutual funds - SEBI is the regulator; AMFI is the industry association.
Going straight to SEBI with a complaint without first approaching the AMC or RTA.
Assuming changes to fundamental attributes need only trustee approval; SEBI approval and a load-free exit window are also required.
Mixing up ACE (code for AMCs) and the distributor code of conduct.
items.recap: SEBI regulates under the SEBI (MF) Regulations; AMFI registers distributors and sets codes but is not a regulator. Distributors must disclose commissions and sell suitably. Investors are entitled to timely payments and documents. Fundamental changes need approvals and a free exit. Complaints: AMC/RTA, then SCORES, then SMART ODR.

items.title: Basics of Derivatives: NISM VIII Revision Notes
items.description: Forwards, futures, options and swaps, OTC vs exchange-traded contracts, market participants and derivative risks - NISM Series VIII revision notes.
items.intro: The first chapter of NISM Series VIII defines derivatives, traces their history in India and introduces the main contract types and participants. Questions are conceptual: identify the instrument from its description, distinguish OTC from exchange-traded contracts, and classify a trader as a hedger, speculator or arbitrageur.

points.heading: What is a derivative
points.text: A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset - a share, index, currency, commodity or interest rate. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 includes derivatives within the definition of securities, which is why SEBI regulates exchange-traded equity derivatives in India.

points.heading: Four basic types
points.text: Forwards are customised bilateral agreements to buy or sell later at a fixed price. Futures are standardised, exchange-traded forwards. Options give the buyer a right, without obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put). Swaps exchange cash-flow streams, such as fixed for floating interest payments.

points.heading: OTC vs exchange-traded
points.text: OTC contracts are negotiated privately, so terms can be tailored, but each party faces the other's default risk and prices are less transparent. Exchange-traded contracts are standardised, cleared through a clearing corporation that guarantees settlement, and marked to market daily.

points.heading: History in India
points.text: Index futures began trading in June 2000 on the Nifty and Sensex, following the L.C. Gupta Committee's recommendations. Index options followed in 2001, then stock options and stock futures. The J.R. Varma Committee laid down the risk containment framework of margins and limits.

points.heading: Hedgers
points.text: Hedgers use derivatives to reduce an existing risk. A fund manager holding ₹10 crore of shares who fears a fall can sell index futures; losses on the portfolio are then offset by gains on the futures. Hedging gives up some upside in return for protection.

points.heading: Speculators
points.text: Speculators take positions to profit from expected price moves, accepting risk. Derivatives give leverage: a margin of perhaps 15% to 20% controls the full contract value, so a 5% move can mean a 25% to 35% gain or loss on capital deployed.

points.heading: Arbitrageurs
points.text: Arbitrageurs exploit price differences between markets. If a stock trades at ₹1,000 in the cash market and its one-month future at ₹1,030 when fair value is ₹1,008, the arbitrageur buys cash and sells futures, locking in the mispricing. Their activity keeps prices aligned.

points.heading: Economic functions
points.text: Derivatives aid price discovery, transfer risk from those who want to shed it to those willing to bear it, increase market liquidity and reduce transaction costs compared with trading the underlying. They also encourage informed participation in the cash market.

points.heading: Risks of derivatives
points.text: Leverage magnifies losses; OTC contracts carry counterparty risk; complex products can be mispriced or misunderstood. SEBI studies have found that most individual traders in equity F&O lose money, a point every distributor and investor should take seriously. Position sizing and stop-losses are essential.

traps: Treating a forward and a future as identical - futures are standardised, exchange-traded and marked to market daily; forwards are customised OTC deals.
Saying an option buyer has an obligation; only the seller has an obligation, the buyer has a right.
Classifying an investor who sells futures against an existing portfolio as a speculator - that is hedging.
Forgetting that index futures, not stock options, were the first equity derivative launched in India (June 2000).
items.recap: A derivative's value comes from an underlying. Forwards are custom OTC, futures standardised on exchange, options give rights, swaps exchange cash flows. Hedgers reduce risk, speculators take it, arbitrageurs exploit mispricing. India started with index futures in 2000. Leverage cuts both ways.

items.title: Stock Market Index Basics: NISM VIII Revision Notes
items.description: Free-float market cap weighting, index calculation, impact cost, Nifty 50 and Sensex, and why indices underlie derivatives - NISM VIII notes.
items.intro: Index derivatives are the most actively traded equity derivatives in India, so Series VIII explains how an index is built. Questions test weighting methods, the free-float concept, index maintenance, and what makes a good index for derivatives, sometimes with a small calculation of index value change.

points.heading: What an index measures
points.text: An index tracks the value of a basket of stocks relative to a base period, showing how the market or a segment has moved. The Nifty 50 started at a base value of 1,000 in November 1995; the Sensex at 100 with 1978-79 as the base year.

points.heading: Free-float market capitalisation
points.text: Most Indian indices use free-float market cap weighting: only shares available for trading are counted, excluding promoter holdings and other locked-in shares. A company with ₹1 lakh crore total market cap but 50% promoter holding contributes only about ₹50,000 crore to index weight.

points.heading: Other weighting methods
points.text: Price-weighted indices (like the Dow Jones Industrial Average) give more weight to high-priced stocks. Equal-weighted indices give every stock the same weight, increasing the influence of smaller companies. Full market cap weighting ignores free float. Nifty and Sensex use neither; both are free-float weighted.

points.heading: Index calculation
points.text: Index value = current free-float market value of constituents / base market value x base index value. The divisor is adjusted for corporate actions such as rights issues or constituent changes, so the index does not jump simply because the basket changed.

points.heading: Index maintenance
points.text: Index providers periodically review constituents for eligibility - size, liquidity, free float and listing history. Stocks are replaced when they no longer qualify. Bonus issues and stock splits do not change market cap and need no divisor adjustment. Changes are announced in advance so index funds can rebalance.

points.heading: Impact cost
points.text: Impact cost measures liquidity: the percentage difference between the actual execution price for a given order size and the ideal mid-price. Lower impact cost means a more liquid stock. Index inclusion criteria often require low impact cost so that the index is tradable.

points.heading: Desirable index attributes
points.text: A good index for derivatives is well diversified, made of liquid stocks, has low impact cost, captures the market's behaviour and is professionally maintained. Diversification reduces manipulation risk and makes the index a good hedge for broad portfolios. A narrow sectoral index is less suitable as a hedge for a diversified portfolio.

points.heading: Uses of an index
points.text: Indices serve as benchmarks for mutual funds, underlyings for index funds, ETFs and derivatives, and barometers of the economy. Index futures and options let investors hedge or take a view on the whole market without buying every stock. Index derivatives also avoid stock-specific risk.

formulas: Index value = (Current market value / Base market value) x Base index value
Free-float market cap = Share price x Shares outstanding x Investable weight factor
traps: Assuming a stock split or bonus issue changes a company's index weight - market cap is unchanged, so weight stays the same.
Confusing impact cost (a liquidity measure) with brokerage or transaction charges.
Thinking promoter holdings are included in free-float weights; they are excluded.
Believing a price-weighted index gives more weight to larger companies; it favours higher-priced shares.
items.recap: Indian indices are free-float market cap weighted. Index = current value / base value x base index. The divisor adjusts for corporate actions; splits and bonuses need none. Impact cost measures liquidity - lower is better. Good derivative indices are diversified, liquid and well maintained.

items.title: Forwards and Futures Pricing: NISM VIII Revision Notes
items.description: Forward vs futures, cost of carry pricing, basis, contango and backwardation, contract specifications and payoffs - NISM Series VIII revision notes.
items.intro: This is a high-weight chapter with frequent numerical questions. It covers the difference between forwards and futures, contract terminology, how futures are priced using cost of carry, the basis, and the linear payoff of long and short futures positions. Practise fair value and MTM calculations until they are automatic.

points.heading: Forward contracts
points.text: A forward is a private agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date. Terms are customised, there is no daily settlement and each party bears the other's credit risk. Forwards are illiquid because exiting requires the counterparty's consent.

points.heading: Futures contracts
points.text: Futures are standardised forwards traded on exchanges: lot size, expiry and settlement are fixed. A clearing corporation becomes counterparty to both sides, and positions are marked to market daily. Traders can exit any time by taking an opposite position. Daily MTM limits the build-up of losses.

points.heading: Key terminology
points.text: Spot price is the current cash market price; futures price is the agreed price; expiry is the last trading day; contract size is lot size times price; basis is spot minus futures. Index and stock futures in India commonly have near, next and far monthly contracts.

points.heading: Cost of carry pricing
points.text: Fair futures price = spot x (1 + r x t) minus the value of dividends expected before expiry, or with continuous compounding F = S x e^(rt). With Nifty at 24,000, a 7% annual rate and one month left, fair value is about 24,000 x (1 + 0.07/12) = 24,140.

points.heading: Contango and backwardation
points.text: When futures trade above spot, the market is in contango, the normal situation for financial assets with positive carry. When futures trade below spot - often due to large expected dividends or strong bearish sentiment - the market is in backwardation. Basis converges to zero at expiry.

points.heading: Long futures payoff
points.text: A buyer of futures gains one rupee for each rupee rise in the underlying and loses one rupee for each rupee fall. Buying a stock future at ₹500 with a lot of 1,000 shares and selling at ₹520 earns ₹20,000, before costs. The payoff is linear and theoretically unlimited both ways.

points.heading: Short futures payoff
points.text: A seller profits when prices fall. Selling at ₹500 and buying back at ₹470 gains ₹30 per share. Losses are theoretically unlimited if prices rise sharply, which is why margins are collected from both buyers and sellers of futures. Short sellers face margin calls on rallies.

points.heading: Settlement styles
points.text: Index futures in India are cash settled on expiry using the closing index value. Stock futures are physically settled: positions open at expiry result in actual delivery of shares, a rule SEBI introduced in phases from 2018. Traders not wanting delivery must close positions before expiry.

points.heading: Expiry and contract changes
points.text: SEBI reviews lot sizes, weekly expiries and expiry days periodically; since 2025 each exchange has one fixed expiry day for its equity derivatives. Learn the concepts and check the current contract specifications on NSE and BSE websites, as of 2026.

formulas: Fair futures price F = S x (1 + r x t) - PV of dividends
Continuous compounding: F = S x e^(r x t)
Basis = Spot price - Futures price
Futures P&L = (Exit price - Entry price) x Lot size for a long position
traps: Defining basis as futures minus spot - the workbook defines basis as spot minus futures, so it is usually negative in contango.
Forgetting to subtract expected dividends when pricing stock or index futures.
Assuming stock futures are cash settled; they are physically settled in India.
Thinking only the futures seller pays margin - both sides do, because both can lose.
items.recap: Forwards are custom OTC deals with counterparty risk; futures are standardised, cleared and marked to market. Fair value = spot plus carry minus dividends. Contango: futures above spot; backwardation: below. Basis converges to zero at expiry. Payoffs are linear. Index futures cash settled, stock futures physically settled.

items.title: Options, Moneyness and Greeks: NISM VIII Revision Notes
items.description: Calls and puts, payoffs, intrinsic and time value, moneyness, put-call parity, Black-Scholes inputs and option Greeks - revision notes for NISM VIII.
items.intro: Options carry the most weight in Series VIII. You must handle payoffs for all four positions, compute intrinsic and time value, identify moneyness, apply put-call parity and know what each Greek measures. Expect several calculation questions; work through each with a small table of prices to avoid sign errors.

points.heading: Rights and obligations
points.text: A call gives the buyer the right to buy the underlying at the strike price; a put gives the right to sell. The buyer pays a premium and has no further obligation. The seller (writer) receives the premium and must perform if the buyer exercises, so the seller pays margin.

points.heading: Payoff of a long call
points.text: Buying a ₹500 call for ₹20: at expiry with the stock at ₹540, profit is 540 - 500 - 20 = ₹20 per share. Break-even is strike plus premium, ₹520. Below ₹500 the option expires worthless and the loss is limited to the ₹20 premium.

points.heading: Payoff of a long put
points.text: Buying a ₹500 put for ₹15 gains when the price falls. At ₹460, profit is 500 - 460 - 15 = ₹25. Break-even is strike minus premium, ₹485. Maximum profit is strike minus premium if the price falls to zero; maximum loss is the premium.

points.heading: Writers' risk
points.text: A call writer's loss is theoretically unlimited because prices can rise without limit. A put writer's maximum loss is strike minus premium. Writers' maximum gain is the premium received, which is why selling options without hedges is risky despite frequent small wins.

points.heading: Moneyness
points.text: A call is in-the-money when spot is above strike, at-the-money when they are equal and out-of-the-money when spot is below strike. For puts, the reverse: a ₹500 put is in-the-money when the stock is at ₹480. Only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.

points.heading: Intrinsic and time value
points.text: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. With spot ₹540, a ₹500 call priced at ₹55 has intrinsic value ₹40 and time value ₹15. Time value decays as expiry nears and is zero at expiry. Out-of-the-money options consist entirely of time value.

points.heading: Option pricing inputs
points.text: The Black-Scholes model uses spot price, strike price, time to expiry, volatility and the risk-free rate (plus dividends). Higher volatility raises both call and put premiums. A higher spot raises call premiums and lowers put premiums; a higher strike does the opposite.

points.heading: Put-call parity
points.text: For European options on the same underlying, strike and expiry: call + present value of strike = put + spot. If the call is ₹30, put ₹20, spot ₹500 and PV of strike ₹490, parity holds because 30 + 490 = 20 + 500. A violation creates an arbitrage opportunity.

points.heading: The Greeks
points.text: Delta measures premium change for a ₹1 change in the underlying (calls 0 to 1, puts 0 to -1). Gamma measures the change in delta. Theta measures time decay, usually negative for buyers. Vega measures sensitivity to volatility. Rho measures sensitivity to interest rates.

points.heading: Exercise styles in India
points.text: Index and stock options on Indian exchanges are European style and can be exercised only on expiry. In-the-money stock options are physically settled, while index options are cash settled. Exchanges automatically exercise in-the-money options at expiry. Stock options moved from American to European style in 2011, so early exercise is no longer possible for any equity option.

formulas: Call payoff at expiry = max(0, S - K) - premium; break-even = K + premium
Put payoff at expiry = max(0, K - S) - premium; break-even = K - premium
Premium = Intrinsic value + Time value
Put-call parity: C + K/(1+r)^t = P + S
traps: Calling a call with spot below strike 'in-the-money' - for calls, in-the-money means spot above strike; puts are the reverse.
Adding premium to strike for a put's break-even; for puts, subtract the premium.
Assuming time value can be negative or remains at expiry - it is zero at expiry.
Thinking option buyers must deposit margin like sellers; buyers pay only the premium.
items.recap: Calls: right to buy; puts: right to sell; buyers risk only the premium, writers carry obligations. Call break-even = strike + premium; put = strike - premium. Premium = intrinsic + time value. Volatility raises both premiums. Put-call parity: C + PV(K) = P + S. Know delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho. Indian options are European.

items.chapter: Strategies using Equity Futures and Options
items.title: F&O Hedging and Option Strategies: NISM VIII Notes
items.description: Hedging with index futures and beta, covered calls, protective puts, spreads, straddles and strangles with payoffs worked out for NISM VIII revision.
items.intro: This chapter applies futures and options to real situations: hedging portfolios, generating income, and expressing views on direction or volatility. Exam questions give strike prices and premiums and ask for maximum profit, maximum loss or break-even, or ask which strategy fits a view. Draw quick payoff tables to avoid errors.

points.heading: Hedging with futures and beta
points.text: Number of futures contracts = portfolio value x beta / (futures price x lot size). A ₹2 crore portfolio with beta 1.2, index futures at 24,000 and an illustrative lot of 50 needs 2,00,00,000 x 1.2 / (24,000 x 50) = 20 contracts sold to hedge fully. Use the exchange's current lot size in practice.

points.heading: Long stock plus short futures
points.text: An investor holding shares who sells the same stock's futures locks in the futures price; gains and losses offset. Beta-weighted index hedges protect against market risk but leave stock-specific risk, since the portfolio may not move exactly with the index.

points.heading: Protective put
points.text: Buying a put on shares already held sets a floor: holding Nifty-linked investments and buying an at-the-money put means losses below the strike are offset, while upside remains open minus the premium paid. It works like insurance and costs the premium.

points.heading: Covered call
points.text: Holding shares and selling an out-of-the-money call earns premium income but caps upside at the strike. Holding a stock at ₹1,000 and selling a ₹1,100 call for ₹25 yields ₹25 extra if the price stays below ₹1,100, but gains above ₹1,100 are given up.

points.heading: Bull call spread
points.text: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call of the same expiry. Buying the 100 call at ₹6 and selling the 110 call at ₹2 costs ₹4 net. Maximum profit = 10 - 4 = ₹6; maximum loss = ₹4; break-even = 104. It suits a moderately bullish view.

points.heading: Bear put spread
points.text: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put. It profits from a moderate fall, with both profit and loss capped. Maximum profit equals the difference between strikes minus net premium paid; maximum loss is the net premium. Buying the 100 put at ₹7 and selling the 90 put at ₹2 costs ₹5, giving a maximum profit of ₹5 and break-even at 95.

points.heading: Long straddle and strangle
points.text: A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike; a long strangle buys an out-of-the-money call and put at different strikes. Both profit from big moves in either direction, for example before a major result or policy announcement. Strangles are cheaper but need a larger move.

points.heading: Short straddle and strangle
points.text: Selling both options earns premium when the market stays range-bound, but losses can be very large if prices move sharply. Straddle break-evens are strike plus and minus the total premium received. A short strangle widens the profit range but collects less premium. Both strategies need disciplined risk management and higher margins, since writers face open-ended exposure on at least one side.

points.heading: Butterfly and calendar spreads
points.text: A long call butterfly buys one lower and one higher strike call and sells two middle-strike calls, profiting if the price ends near the middle strike with limited risk. A calendar spread sells a near-month option or future and buys a far-month one, trading the time difference.

points.heading: Arbitrage strategies
points.text: Cash-futures arbitrage buys in the cash market and sells futures when futures trade above fair value, earning risk-free carry - this is how arbitrage funds work. Reverse arbitrage sells cash and buys futures when futures are underpriced. Returns shrink as more arbitrageurs compete.

formulas: Hedge contracts = (Portfolio value x Beta) / (Futures price x Lot size)
Bull call spread: max profit = strike difference - net debit; max loss = net debit
Long straddle break-evens = Strike +/- total premium paid
traps: Ignoring beta when hedging - a high-beta portfolio needs more index futures than its rupee value suggests.
Thinking a covered call protects against falls; it only offsets the fall by the premium received.
Using a straddle when the view is directional; straddles profit from volatility, not a specific direction.
Calculating spread maximum profit without subtracting the net premium paid.
items.recap: Hedge size = portfolio x beta / (futures price x lot). Protective put = insurance; covered call = income with capped upside. Bull call and bear put spreads limit both profit and loss. Long straddles and strangles bet on big moves; short ones bet on calm markets with large risk. Arbitrage keeps futures near fair value.

items.title: F&O Trading Mechanism and Order Types: NISM VIII
items.description: Trading system, order types, member categories, client identification, position limits and market-wide limits for equity derivatives - NISM VIII notes.
items.intro: This chapter explains how derivative orders are placed and matched on Indian exchanges, the types of members, order conditions and the limits that control excessive positions. Questions are factual: which order type behaves how, who a clearing member is, and what happens when a stock crosses its market-wide position limit.

points.heading: Screen-based trading
points.text: NSE's derivatives segment uses an anonymous, order-driven electronic system (NEAT and its successors), and BSE uses BOLT Plus. Orders are matched on price-time priority: the best price first, and among equal prices, the earliest order first. Members access the system through terminals and approved APIs.

points.heading: Member categories
points.text: Trading members execute trades for themselves and clients. Clearing members clear and settle trades. Trading-cum-clearing members do both. Professional clearing members (often banks or custodians) clear and settle trades of other trading members but do not trade themselves. Each category has separate net worth requirements.

points.heading: Order types
points.text: A limit order executes at the specified price or better. A market order executes immediately at the best available price. A stop-loss order becomes active only when the trigger price is reached, then becomes a limit or market order. Exchanges may restrict market orders in illiquid contracts.

points.heading: Time and other conditions
points.text: Day orders are valid until the end of the trading day. Immediate or Cancel (IOC) orders execute fully or partly at once and any unfilled portion is cancelled. Exchanges in India generally do not allow orders to remain beyond the day for derivatives.

points.heading: Client identification
points.text: Every order must carry the client's Unique Client Code, registered with the exchange along with PAN. Brokers must complete KYC, a client registration form and a risk disclosure document before a client trades. Pro orders (for the member's own account) must be distinguished from client orders.

points.heading: Eligibility of stocks
points.text: SEBI sets criteria for stocks to have derivatives: market capitalisation, average daily turnover and delivery value, and market-wide position limits, among others. Stocks failing the criteria for a set period are excluded from F&O after existing contracts expire. Check current criteria with SEBI.

points.heading: Market-wide position limit
points.text: Each stock has a market-wide position limit (MWPL) based on its free float or delivery data. When open interest crosses 95% of MWPL, the stock enters a ban period: no fresh positions are allowed, only positions that reduce exposure, until open interest falls below 80%.

points.heading: Client and member limits
points.text: Exchanges set position limits at client, trading member and market-wide levels for index and stock derivatives. These prevent any single participant from cornering a contract. Limits for index derivatives are generally higher than for individual stocks. Breaches attract penalties and forced reduction of positions.

points.heading: Base price and price bands
points.text: Derivative contracts have operating ranges; orders outside the range are rejected or need confirmation. Index futures have flexible price bands tied to the underlying's movement. Options do not have fixed price bands but have operating ranges to prevent fat-finger errors.

traps: Thinking a professional clearing member can trade on its own account - it only clears and settles for trading members.
Believing a stop-loss order is executed immediately; it waits until the trigger price is touched.
Assuming existing positions must be closed during an F&O ban; only fresh positions are barred.
Mixing up the 95% trigger that starts a ban with the 80% level that ends it.
items.recap: Orders match on price-time priority in anonymous electronic systems. Trading members trade, clearing members settle, PCMs only clear. Limit, market, stop-loss, day and IOC orders behave differently. Every order needs a UCC. F&O ban starts when open interest crosses 95% of MWPL and ends below 80%.

items.title: Derivatives Clearing, Margins and Settlement: NISM VIII
items.description: Novation, clearing corporation role, initial and exposure margin, SPAN, MTM settlement, final settlement and the Core SGF explained for NISM VIII.
items.intro: Clearing and settlement ensures that every derivatives trade is honoured. This chapter covers the clearing corporation's role, margin types, daily mark-to-market, final settlement of futures and options, and default protections. Expect calculation questions on MTM plus conceptual questions on novation and margins.

points.heading: Clearing corporations
points.text: NSE Clearing Ltd and Indian Clearing Corporation Ltd (for BSE) clear equity derivatives. Through novation, the clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, so participants never face each other's default risk. This guarantee is what makes exchange-traded contracts safer than OTC ones.

points.heading: Initial margin and SPAN
points.text: Initial margin covers the potential one-day loss of a portfolio under adverse scenarios. It is computed with SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk), which evaluates the portfolio across price and volatility scenarios. Margins are collected upfront before positions are taken.

points.heading: Exposure margin
points.text: Exposure (extreme loss) margin is collected in addition to initial margin to cover risks beyond those captured by SPAN. Index derivatives generally have lower exposure margin than stock derivatives because indices are less volatile. It is usually a fixed percentage of the notional contract value, added on top of SPAN.

points.heading: Mark-to-market settlement
points.text: Futures positions are revalued daily at the settlement price, and profits or losses are settled in cash the next day. A trader long 1 lot of 1,000 shares bought at ₹500, with a settlement price of ₹508, receives ₹8,000 MTM profit; his new cost becomes ₹508.

points.heading: Final settlement
points.text: On expiry, index futures and options are cash settled at the final settlement price (the closing value of the underlying). Stock futures and in-the-money stock options are physically settled through delivery of shares, so margins rise as expiry approaches for delivery obligations.

points.heading: Premium settlement
points.text: Options premium is paid by the buyer and received by the seller on a T+1 basis. Option buyers pay only premium; sellers pay initial and exposure margins because they carry open-ended risk. Writers' premium receipts can count towards margins only as exchange rules permit, and buyers' premiums must be paid in full before trading.

points.heading: Settlement Guarantee Fund
points.text: Each clearing corporation maintains a Core Settlement Guarantee Fund to complete settlement if a member defaults. Contributions come from the clearing corporation, the exchange and clearing members, as per SEBI norms. Its size is reviewed regularly through stress tests that assume the default of the largest members under extreme but plausible market conditions.

points.heading: Risk controls
points.text: Clearing corporations monitor positions in real time, apply position limits, and can square off positions of members whose margins are insufficient. Brokers must collect margins from clients upfront; shortfalls attract penalties. Client funds and collateral must be segregated from the broker's own.

points.heading: Spread margin benefit
points.text: A calendar spread - long near month, short far month of the same underlying - carries much lower risk than two outright positions because the legs offset. Clearing corporations therefore charge a reduced margin on recognised spreads. The benefit is withdrawn as the near leg approaches expiry.

formulas: Daily MTM = (Today's settlement price - Previous settlement price or trade price) x Quantity
traps: Thinking clearing members bear each other's default risk - novation makes the clearing corporation the counterparty.
Assuming option buyers pay SPAN margin; they pay premium, while sellers pay margin.
Believing MTM is settled only at expiry; it is settled daily.
Confusing the Core SGF (protects settlement against member default) with the Investor Protection Fund (compensates investors).
items.recap: Novation makes the clearing corporation counterparty to all. Initial margin via SPAN plus exposure margin, collected upfront. Futures MTM settled daily in cash. Index derivatives cash settled; stock derivatives physically settled. Buyers pay premium, sellers pay margin. Core SGF backs settlement. Spreads get margin relief.

items.title: Equity Derivatives Regulation in India: NISM VIII Notes
items.description: SCRA, SEBI Act, L.C. Gupta and J.R. Varma committees, eligibility of members and SEBI's investor protection measures for F&O - NISM VIII revision.
items.intro: This chapter covers the laws and committees behind India's equity derivatives market and SEBI's regulatory role. It is a short chapter in the exam but easy marks if you remember which law covers what and which committee recommended what.

points.heading: Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956
points.text: The SCRA governs stock exchanges and contracts in securities. Its definition of 'securities' was amended in 1999 to include derivatives, making them legal to trade on recognised exchanges. Derivatives must be traded on a recognised exchange and settled through its clearing corporation.

points.heading: SEBI Act, 1992
points.text: The SEBI Act gives SEBI its mandate to protect investors, develop the securities market and regulate it. SEBI registers intermediaries such as brokers and clearing members, frames regulations, conducts inspections and can impose penalties or bar entities from the market.

points.heading: SC(R) Rules, 1957
points.text: The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules lay down requirements such as listing conditions and the contents of contracts. Together with SEBI regulations and exchange bye-laws, they form the legal framework within which derivatives segments operate. Exchange bye-laws add operational detail such as trading hours, member conduct and arbitration of disputes between members and clients.

points.heading: L.C. Gupta Committee
points.text: SEBI's L.C. Gupta Committee (report in 1998) recommended introducing exchange-traded derivatives, starting with index futures, and suggested that derivatives segments be separate from cash segments with their own governing councils and clearing arrangements. It also recommended that the derivatives exchange or segment have a separate clearing corporation or house, and that members meet higher capital requirements than cash-market brokers.

points.heading: J.R. Varma Committee
points.text: The J.R. Varma Committee framed the risk containment measures for derivatives: margins based on value at risk, mark-to-market settlement, position limits and the methodology for setting margins. These ideas still underpin today's risk management. It recommended a 99% value-at-risk approach for initial margins and a liquid net worth requirement for clearing members, ensuring members could absorb losses without delaying settlement.

points.heading: Exchange and member requirements
points.text: Exchanges need SEBI approval to start derivatives segments. Trading and clearing members must meet net worth and other eligibility conditions, have certified staff (NISM Series VIII for associated persons) and follow exchange rules on client dealing. Members must also maintain records, submit periodic reports to the exchange and undergo regular inspections by the exchange and SEBI.

points.heading: Self-regulation by exchanges
points.text: Exchanges act as first-level regulators: they admit members, monitor trading through surveillance systems, impose penalties for violations and can suspend members. SEBI oversees the exchanges and clearing corporations themselves, while market infrastructure institutions must meet SEBI's governance and ownership norms.

points.heading: Recent investor protection measures
points.text: Responding to studies showing large losses by individual traders, SEBI has tightened rules on index derivatives - larger contract sizes, fewer weekly expiries, upfront collection of option premium and intraday monitoring of position limits. Details change; check SEBI circulars as of 2026.

traps: Attributing risk containment measures to the L.C. Gupta Committee - those came from the J.R. Varma Committee.
Thinking derivatives were legal before the 1999 SCRA amendment; that amendment brought them within 'securities'.
Assuming RBI regulates equity derivatives; SEBI does.
Forgetting that associated persons dealing in equity derivatives need NISM Series VIII certification.
items.recap: SCRA 1956, amended in 1999, made derivatives 'securities'. SEBI Act 1992 empowers SEBI. L.C. Gupta recommended starting derivatives with index futures; J.R. Varma designed margins and risk controls. Members need net worth and certified staff. SEBI keeps tightening F&O rules to protect individual traders.

items.title: F&O Accounting and Taxation: NISM VIII Revision Notes
items.description: ICAI guidance for futures and options accounting, business income treatment, STT on derivatives, turnover and set-off of losses for NISM VIII.
items.intro: This chapter covers how futures and options are accounted for and taxed in India. Questions are few but predictable: business income versus speculation, how STT applies, and how margins and premiums appear in the books. Tax rates and STT rates change, so learn the structure and check current rates for 2026.

points.heading: Accounting for futures
points.text: As per ICAI's guidance, initial margin paid is shown as a current asset ('initial margin - equity derivatives'). Daily MTM receipts and payments go through a mark-to-market margin account, and the net profit or loss on settlement or squaring off is recognised in the profit and loss account.

points.heading: Accounting for options
points.text: Premium paid by the buyer is shown as an asset until the option is exercised, squared off or expires. Premium received by the writer is shown as a liability until then. On expiry or squaring off, the difference is taken to the profit and loss account; open positions may need provisions for losses.

points.heading: Business, not speculative, income
points.text: Trading in equity derivatives on a recognised stock exchange is excluded from 'speculative transaction' under the Income-tax law. Profits are therefore taxed as non-speculative business income at slab rates, and losses can be set off against other business income (not salary) and carried forward for eight years.

points.heading: Securities Transaction Tax
points.text: STT applies to equity derivatives: on the sale of futures based on traded price, on the sale of options based on premium, and a higher rate on the intrinsic value of options exercised. STT rates have been raised in recent Budgets - check current rates with the income tax department as of 2026.

points.heading: Turnover for tax audit
points.text: For F&O traders, turnover is generally computed as the sum of absolute profits and losses on trades (plus premium on options sold, as per ICAI guidance), not the notional contract value. Turnover determines tax audit applicability. Audit thresholds are set in the Act; check the current limits.

points.heading: Expenses and deductions
points.text: Since F&O income is business income, related expenses - brokerage, internet, advisory subscriptions, depreciation on computers - can be claimed. STT paid is also allowed as a deduction when computing business income. Keeping clean records of each trade, contract note and expense makes computing business income and filing the return far easier at year end.

points.heading: Disclosure in financial statements
points.text: Entities holding open derivative positions at the balance sheet date should disclose the number of contracts, underlying, long or short side and the margin balances. Investors and auditors use these disclosures to judge the size of derivative exposure relative to the business, since notional values can be large compared with the margins paid.

points.heading: Hedging transactions
points.text: Derivatives used to hedge holdings in the same securities are also treated as non-speculative under the exclusion. Gains on the underlying shares, however, remain capital gains, so a hedger may have business income or loss on futures and capital gains on shares.

traps: Calling exchange-traded F&O profits 'speculative income' - they are non-speculative business income.
Using total contract value as turnover; the absolute sum of profits and losses is used.
Recording option premium paid as an immediate expense; it is carried as an asset until exercise, expiry or squaring off.
Assuming STT applies equally to buyers and sellers of options; it is mainly on the sell side and on exercise.
items.recap: Initial margin is a current asset; MTM flows through a margin account. Option premium paid is an asset, received is a liability, until closure. Exchange-traded F&O income is non-speculative business income; losses set off against business income and carried forward eight years. STT applies on sale and exercise; rates change - check current ones.

items.title: F&O Sales Practices and Investor Protection: NISM VIII
items.description: Know your client, suitability, risk disclosure, broker conduct, investor grievance redressal via SCORES and SMART ODR and the IPF - NISM VIII revision notes.
items.intro: This chapter focuses on how brokers must deal with derivatives clients: KYC, assessing suitability, risk disclosure, fair conduct and handling complaints. Questions test the documents a client must receive and the escalation path for grievances.

points.heading: Know your client
points.text: Before trading, brokers must complete KYC through a KRA, collect PAN and verify identity, and capture income and net worth details. Clients trading F&O must provide proof of financial capacity, such as income tax returns, salary slips or bank statements, before the segment is activated.

points.heading: Suitability
points.text: Derivatives are leveraged and complex. Brokers should assess whether a client understands the products and can bear losses, and should not encourage inexperienced clients to trade F&O. Unsolicited tips promising profits are a sales malpractice. Brokers must also review clients' financial details periodically, particularly when trading volumes rise sharply compared with declared income.

points.heading: Risk disclosure document
points.text: Every client must receive the Risk Disclosure Document explaining leverage, margin calls, the possibility of losing more than the initial margin and the risks of options writing. SEBI also requires brokers to show a risk disclosure on F&O losses to clients, based on SEBI's studies.

points.heading: Fair dealing
points.text: Brokers must execute orders as instructed, send contract notes within the prescribed time, settle client funds periodically and segregate client money and securities. Trading in clients' accounts without authorisation and misusing client collateral are serious violations. Clients should check contract notes and the exchange's trade verification alerts sent by SMS and email.

points.heading: Margin and collateral rules
points.text: Client margins must be collected upfront and reported to the exchange; client securities pledged as margin stay in the client's demat account via the margin pledge system rather than being transferred to the broker. This reduces misuse. Clients can verify their balances through statements from the exchange and depository.

points.heading: Grievance redressal
points.text: A client should first complain to the broker. If not satisfied, the complaint can be escalated to the exchange's investor service cell and to SEBI through SCORES, and then resolved through the SMART ODR platform for online conciliation and arbitration.

points.heading: Avoiding tips and finfluencers
points.text: SEBI has barred regulated entities such as brokers from associating with unregistered persons who give investment advice or make claims about returns, including many social media 'finfluencers'. Clients should treat promises of sure-shot option profits, paid tip groups and requests to share login credentials as red flags and report them.

points.heading: Investor Protection Fund
points.text: Exchanges maintain an Investor Protection Fund to compensate investors with legitimate claims when a broker is declared a defaulter, up to specified limits. The IPF does not cover trading losses from market movements. Claims are scrutinised by the exchange's committee before any payout is approved, and limits per investor are reviewed periodically.

traps: Thinking the IPF compensates trading losses - it covers claims against defaulting brokers only.
Skipping the broker and going straight to SMART ODR; the broker and SCORES come first.
Believing a client cannot lose more than the margin deposited; futures losses can exceed initial margin.
Assuming F&O can be activated with only PAN and address proof; proof of financial capacity is required.
items.recap: KYC plus proof of income before F&O activation. Assess suitability, give the Risk Disclosure Document and never promise profits. Segregate client funds; margins stay pledged in client demat. Complaints: broker, then exchange/SCORES, then SMART ODR. IPF pays for broker defaults, not market losses.

items.title: Financial Planning Basics for NISM X-A: Revision Notes
items.description: The financial planning process, life cycle stages, goal setting, risk profiling and the adviser-client relationship - revision notes for NISM X-A.
items.intro: NISM X-A opens with what investment advice and financial planning involve: the step-by-step planning process, how a client's needs change across the life cycle, and how goals are framed. Questions test the order of planning steps, the difference between advice and product selling, and how to prioritise competing goals.

points.heading: What investment advice means
points.text: Under SEBI rules, investment advice is advice on investing in, buying, selling or dealing in securities or investment products, including financial planning, given for consideration. A registered adviser acts in the client's interest and is paid by the client, unlike a distributor who earns commission from product providers.

points.heading: The planning process
points.text: The standard sequence is: establish the client relationship and scope, gather data and understand goals, analyse the current financial position, develop and present recommendations, implement them, and monitor and review. Data gathering and analysis must come before any product recommendation.

points.heading: Quantitative and qualitative data
points.text: Quantitative data covers income, expenses, assets, liabilities, insurance and existing investments. Qualitative data covers attitudes to risk, family values, health, career prospects and preferences. Both are needed: two clients with the same numbers may need different advice because of different priorities.

points.heading: Framing goals
points.text: Each goal should be specific, measurable, time-bound and priced in future rupees. 'Child's engineering education in 15 years, costing ₹25 lakh today' is usable; 'save for children' is not. Inflation must be applied to today's cost to find the future target.

points.heading: Prioritising goals
points.text: Riya, 28, wants a house down payment in 3 years, retirement at 58 and her newborn's higher education in 18 years. Near-term goals need safe, liquid assets; long-term goals can use more equity. Essential goals such as emergency funds and insurance come before aspirational ones.

points.heading: Financial life cycle
points.text: Early career: low assets, rising income, long horizon - focus on protection and accumulation. Mid-career: peak earnings and expenses for children and home loans. Pre-retirement: consolidation and reducing risk. Retirement: income generation, capital preservation and estate planning. Advice must evolve as the client moves between stages.

points.heading: Risk profiling
points.text: Risk profile combines risk capacity (objective ability to bear losses, based on income stability, horizon and wealth) and risk tolerance (psychological willingness). When they conflict, advisers should usually lean towards the lower of the two to avoid panic selling later.

points.heading: Role of insurance and contingency
points.text: Before investing for growth, a client needs adequate term life cover, health insurance and an emergency fund of roughly three to six months' expenses. Without these, a medical event or job loss may force premature selling of long-term investments. Insurance is protection, not investment.

formulas: Future cost of a goal = Today's cost x (1 + inflation)^years
traps: Recommending products before completing data gathering and analysis - the process order matters.
Treating risk tolerance and risk capacity as the same thing; capacity is objective, tolerance is attitudinal.
Using today's cost of a goal without adjusting for inflation.
Ignoring insurance and emergency funds while building an investment portfolio.
items.recap: Advice is client-paid and client-first. Planning runs: relationship, data, analysis, recommendations, implementation, review. Goals need amounts in future rupees and dates. Life cycle drives priorities. Risk profile = capacity plus tolerance; use the lower. Insure and build an emergency fund before investing for growth.

items.title: Time Value of Money for NISM X-A: Formulas and Examples
items.description: Future value, present value, annuities, SIP future value, effective annual rate and rule of 72 with worked examples - NISM X-A revision notes.
items.intro: Time value of money underpins almost every calculation in X-A: goal planning, loan EMIs, bond prices and retirement corpus. The exam expects you to compute FV, PV, annuity values and effective rates on a financial calculator or spreadsheet. Practise the worked examples below until you can do them quickly.

points.heading: Why money has time value
points.text: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow because it can be invested to earn a return, and because inflation reduces future purchasing power. Every comparison of cash flows at different dates must bring them to a common point in time.

points.heading: Future value of a lump sum
points.text: ₹1,00,000 invested for 5 years at 8% compounded annually grows to 1,00,000 x 1.08^5 = ₹1,46,933. Compounding more frequently increases the result slightly, since interest starts earning interest sooner. The same amount at 12% for 5 years would grow to about ₹1,76,234, showing how a few percentage points of extra return add up over time.

points.heading: Present value of a lump sum
points.text: To have ₹10,00,000 in 10 years at 7% a year, the client must invest 10,00,000 / 1.07^10 = about ₹5,08,349 today. The higher the discount rate or the longer the period, the lower the present value. At 10%, only about ₹3,85,543 would be needed today.

points.heading: Effective annual rate
points.text: A nominal 12% compounded monthly gives an effective annual rate of (1 + 0.12/12)^12 - 1 = 12.68%. When comparing loans or deposits with different compounding frequencies, compare effective rates, not nominal ones. Quarterly compounding at 12% gives 12.55%, so the more frequent the compounding, the higher the effective rate.

points.heading: Annuities
points.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments at equal intervals. In an ordinary annuity, payments come at the end of each period (most SIPs and EMIs are modelled this way); in an annuity due, at the beginning (rent paid in advance). An annuity due is worth more because each payment compounds one period longer.

points.heading: Future value of a SIP
points.text: ₹10,000 at the end of each month for 10 years at 12% a year (1% a month) grows to 10,000 x [(1.01^120 - 1) / 0.01] = about ₹23 lakh, against ₹12 lakh invested. The extra ₹11 lakh is the effect of compounding.

points.heading: Loan EMIs
points.text: EMI = P x r x (1+r)^n / [(1+r)^n - 1], where r is the monthly rate. A ₹30 lakh home loan at 9% for 20 years has an EMI of about ₹26,992. Early EMIs are mostly interest; the principal share grows over time.

points.heading: Rule of 72
points.text: Dividing 72 by the annual return gives approximate doubling time: at 8%, money doubles in about 9 years; at 12%, in about 6. Clients find it an intuitive way to grasp the power of returns and the cost of high-interest debt.

points.heading: Real rate of return
points.text: Real rate = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1. With 10% nominal and 6% inflation, real return is 3.77%. Retirement planning often discounts expenses at the real rate to find the corpus needed for inflation-adjusted withdrawals. Simple subtraction gives 4%, which overstates it.

formulas: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n;  PV = FV / (1 + r)^n
FV of ordinary annuity = P x [(1 + r)^n - 1] / r
EAR = (1 + i/m)^m - 1, where m is compounding periods per year
Real rate = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1
traps: Using the annual rate with monthly periods - convert to a monthly rate and monthly number of periods.
Confusing annuity due (start of period) with ordinary annuity (end of period).
Comparing nominal rates with different compounding frequencies instead of effective rates.
Subtracting inflation from nominal return when the question asks for the exact real rate.
items.recap: Bring all cash flows to one date. FV = PV(1+r)^n; PV = FV/(1+r)^n. EAR adjusts for compounding frequency. Annuity due beats ordinary annuity by one period of growth. Match rate and period units. Rule of 72 gives doubling time. Use the exact real rate formula when precision is asked.

items.title: Client Net Worth, Cash Flow and Debt: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Personal balance sheet, cash flow statement, net worth, liquidity and debt ratios, EMI affordability and loan prioritisation for NISM X-A revision.
items.intro: Before advising, an adviser must understand where the client stands today. This chapter covers building a personal balance sheet and cash flow statement, key ratios, and how to manage debt sensibly. Questions often give a client's numbers and ask for net worth, a ratio, or the better debt decision.

points.heading: Personal balance sheet
points.text: Assets minus liabilities equals net worth. A client with a house worth ₹60 lakh, mutual funds ₹15 lakh, bank balances ₹5 lakh and a car ₹5 lakh has assets of ₹85 lakh. With a ₹35 lakh home loan, net worth is ₹50 lakh.

points.heading: Types of assets
points.text: Advisers separate personal-use assets (home, car, jewellery worn) from investment assets (equity, debt, investment property) and liquid assets (cash, savings, liquid funds). Only investment and liquid assets can fund goals without lifestyle disruption. A client with ₹1 crore net worth may have only ₹10 lakh truly investable once the home and car are excluded.

points.heading: Cash flow statement
points.text: Monthly or yearly income minus expenses shows the surplus available for investing. Separating fixed obligations (EMIs, rent, premiums) from discretionary spending shows where savings can be increased. A negative surplus signals a need to restructure before investing. Annual items like school fees need monthly provisioning.

points.heading: Liquidity ratio
points.text: Liquid assets divided by monthly expenses shows how many months the client can survive without income. A ratio of three to six is a common rule of thumb; self-employed clients or single-income families may need more. Liquid funds and sweep FDs can hold this reserve.

points.heading: Debt service ratio
points.text: Total EMIs divided by gross monthly income measures loan burden. A client earning ₹1,20,000 with EMIs of ₹30,000 and ₹6,000 has a ratio of 30%. Lenders and planners often treat 35% to 40% as an upper comfort zone, though it varies.

points.heading: Savings ratio
points.text: Savings divided by income shows discipline. A household saving ₹25,000 of ₹1,00,000 monthly income has a 25% savings ratio. Rising income with a flat savings ratio usually means lifestyle inflation, a common issue for mid-career clients. Advisers often set target savings ratios by goal.

points.heading: Good and bad debt
points.text: Debt that finances appreciating or income-producing assets at reasonable rates, like a home loan or education loan, can be productive. High-cost consumer debt - credit card revolving balances at around 36% a year or personal loans for consumption - erodes wealth.

points.heading: Prioritising repayment
points.text: Repay the costliest debt first. A client with a credit card balance at 36% and an FD earning 7% should usually break the FD to clear the card: every rupee repaid 'earns' 36% risk-free. The debt avalanche method targets the highest rate first.

points.heading: Prepayment decisions
points.text: Prepaying a home loan at 8.5% makes sense if expected post-tax investment returns are lower or the client values being debt-free. Tax benefits on home loan interest (where available under the chosen tax regime) lower the effective cost and should be factored in.

formulas: Net worth = Total assets - Total liabilities
Debt service ratio = Total EMIs / Gross monthly income
Liquidity ratio = Liquid assets / Monthly expenses
traps: Counting a car or self-occupied home as an investment asset available for goals.
Keeping a low-yield FD while paying high credit card interest - clearing the card usually wins.
Using net income in the debt service ratio when the question specifies gross income, or vice versa.
Assuming all debt is bad; productive debt at reasonable cost can build assets.
items.recap: Net worth = assets minus liabilities; separate personal-use, investment and liquid assets. Cash flow shows investable surplus. Liquidity ratio of three to six months; debt service ratio ideally under about 40%. Repay costliest debt first, especially credit cards. Prepay loans when effective cost exceeds expected post-tax returns.

items.title: Indian Financial Markets and Regulators: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Money market vs capital market instruments, primary and secondary markets, RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA roles in India's financial system - NISM X-A.
items.intro: This chapter maps India's financial system: the markets, the instruments in each and the regulators who oversee them. Questions ask which regulator governs a market or product and whether an instrument is a money market or capital market security. Clear categorisation is the key to scoring here.

points.heading: Role of financial markets
points.text: Financial markets channel savings from households to businesses and governments that need capital. They provide price discovery, liquidity and risk transfer. Efficient markets lower the cost of capital and give savers access to a wide range of risk-return choices. Without them, capital would sit idle in households.

points.heading: Money market
points.text: The money market deals in short-term funds with maturities up to one year: call money, treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos and TREPS. Participants are mainly banks, primary dealers, mutual funds and large companies. RBI regulates it and uses it to transmit monetary policy.

points.heading: Capital market
points.text: The capital market deals in long-term funds: equity shares, corporate bonds, government securities and their derivatives. It has a primary market for new issues and a secondary market for trading existing securities on stock exchanges. SEBI regulates most of it; RBI regulates the government securities market.

points.heading: Call money and treasury bills
points.text: Call money is overnight interbank borrowing and lending, governed by RBI. Treasury bills are short-term government securities issued at a discount in 91, 182 and 364-day maturities. Their yields indicate short-term interest rates in the economy. T-bills are popular with liquid funds and corporate treasuries for parking short-term cash.

points.heading: Regulators
points.text: RBI regulates banks, NBFCs, money and forex markets and payment systems. SEBI regulates securities markets, mutual funds, brokers and investment advisers. IRDAI regulates insurance; PFRDA regulates NPS and pension funds. IFSCA regulates financial services in GIFT City IFSC. A product can involve more than one regulator.

points.heading: Financial intermediaries
points.text: Banks, NBFCs, mutual funds, insurers, brokers, depositories and investment advisers all act as intermediaries. Each operates under its regulator's licence. Advisers should know which regulator governs a product so they can guide clients on documents, disclosures and grievance routes. This also tells clients where to escalate complaints.

points.heading: Monetary policy link
points.text: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate. A cut usually lowers money market and bond yields, raising bond prices; a hike does the opposite. Advisers track policy to position clients' debt portfolios on duration. Long duration funds gain the most when yields fall, and lose the most when they rise.

points.heading: Government securities market
points.text: G-secs are issued by RBI on behalf of the central government through auctions. Retail investors can buy them directly through RBI Retail Direct or through exchanges. They carry no credit risk but do carry interest rate risk. State development loans are issued by states.

traps: Classifying a five-year corporate bond as a money market instrument - money market covers maturities up to one year.
Naming SEBI as the regulator of the call money market; RBI governs it.
Assuming government securities are free of all risk; they carry interest rate risk.
Mixing up IRDAI (insurance) and PFRDA (pension) jurisdiction over NPS.
items.recap: Money market = up to one year (call money, T-bills, CP, CD, repo), regulated by RBI. Capital market = long term (shares, bonds), mostly SEBI, with G-secs under RBI. Regulators: RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IFSCA. Repo rate moves feed into bond yields. G-secs have no credit risk but do have rate risk.

items.title: Primary and Secondary Securities Markets: NISM X-A
items.description: IPOs, FPOs, rights issues, book building, ASBA, secondary market trading, T+1 settlement and market infrastructure institutions - NISM X-A notes.
items.intro: This chapter explains how securities are first issued and then traded. It covers public issue types, the book-building process, ASBA and UPI, secondary market trading, settlement cycles and the role of exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories. Questions are factual and often about which market a transaction belongs to.

points.heading: Primary market
points.text: The primary market is where securities are issued for the first time and money flows to the issuer. An IPO is a company's first public offer; a follow-on public offer (FPO) is a later one. Rights issues offer shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

points.heading: Offer for sale vs fresh issue
points.text: In a fresh issue, new shares are created and the company receives the money. In an offer for sale, existing shareholders such as promoters or PE funds sell their shares, and the money goes to them, not the company. Many IPOs combine both.

points.heading: Book building
points.text: In book building, investors bid within a price band and the final price is discovered from demand. In a fixed price issue, the price is set in advance. Retail individual investors receive a reserved portion of the issue in book-built IPOs.

points.heading: ASBA and UPI
points.text: Applications Supported by Blocked Amount (ASBA) keep the application money in the investor's bank account, only blocked until allotment. Retail investors can use UPI mandates. Listing happens within a few working days after the issue closes under SEBI's shortened timeline.

points.heading: Private placements and QIPs
points.text: Companies can also raise money through private placements to select investors and qualified institutions placements (QIPs) for listed companies selling to institutional buyers. These are faster and cheaper than public issues but not open to retail investors. Preferential allotments are another such route.

points.heading: Secondary market
points.text: The secondary market is where existing securities are traded between investors on stock exchanges such as NSE and BSE. The company receives no money from these trades. Liquidity in the secondary market makes primary issues attractive. Prices are set by demand and supply among investors.

points.heading: Settlement cycle
points.text: Indian equity cash market trades settle on a T+1 rolling basis, with an optional T+0 cycle introduced for select stocks. Shares are credited to the buyer's demat account and funds to the seller after settlement through the clearing corporation. Shorter cycles reduce counterparty risk.

points.heading: Market infrastructure
points.text: Stock exchanges provide trading platforms; clearing corporations guarantee and settle trades; depositories (NSDL and CDSL) hold securities electronically. Together they are called market infrastructure institutions and are closely regulated by SEBI. Their ownership and governance norms are stricter than for ordinary companies, because the whole market depends on them working without interruption.

traps: Calling an IPO a secondary market transaction - shares are issued fresh, so it is primary.
Assuming the company receives money from an offer for sale; the selling shareholders do.
Quoting T+2 as the current equity settlement cycle; India moved to T+1.
Believing ASBA debits the money at application; it only blocks it until allotment.
items.recap: Primary market = new issues, money to issuer (IPO, FPO, rights, QIP). Offer for sale money goes to selling shareholders. Book building discovers price within a band; ASBA blocks funds.
