Secondary market = trading between investors on exchanges. Equity settles T+1. Exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories form the market infrastructure.

items.title: Equity Valuation and Analysis for NISM X-A: Notes
items.description: P/E, P/B, dividend yield, EPS, corporate actions, market cap categories and fundamental vs technical analysis with examples for NISM X-A revision.
items.intro: Advisers need to understand what drives equity returns and how shares are valued. This chapter covers valuation ratios, corporate actions, market-cap categories and analysis approaches. Expect calculation questions on P/E and dividend yield and conceptual questions on bonus issues, splits and buybacks.

points.heading: Sources of equity return
points.text: Equity returns come from dividends and capital appreciation. Over long periods, earnings growth drives share prices, but in the short term valuation changes and sentiment dominate. Equity has no promised return and ranks last in claims on a company's assets.

points.heading: Price-to-earnings ratio
points.text: P/E = market price / earnings per share. A share at ₹450 with EPS of ₹30 has a P/E of 15. A high P/E may reflect strong growth expectations or overvaluation; comparisons are meaningful only within the same industry and against the company's own history.

points.heading: Price-to-book and dividend yield
points.text: P/B compares price with book value per share and is useful for banks and asset-heavy firms. Dividend yield = dividend per share / price: a ₹12 dividend on a ₹400 share is a 3% yield. High yields may signal value or a falling price.

points.heading: Corporate actions
points.text: A 1:1 bonus issue doubles the number of shares and roughly halves the price, so the shareholder's total value is unchanged. A stock split does the same by reducing face value. Buybacks reduce share count and can raise EPS. Rights issues let existing shareholders buy new shares, usually at a discount.

points.heading: Market cap categories
points.text: SEBI's categorisation used by mutual funds treats the top 100 listed companies by full market capitalisation as large caps, 101 to 250 as mid caps and the rest as small caps. Small caps typically offer higher growth potential with higher volatility and lower liquidity.

points.heading: Fundamental analysis
points.text: Fundamental analysis evaluates the economy, industry and company - revenue growth, margins, return on equity, debt levels, management quality and competitive position - to estimate intrinsic value. Discounted cash flow and dividend discount models are common tools. The aim is to buy below intrinsic value.

points.heading: Technical analysis
points.text: Technical analysis studies price and volume patterns, trends, moving averages and indicators to time entries and exits. It assumes prices reflect all information and trends persist. Advisers generally use it, if at all, as a supplement to fundamental work. Evidence of consistent profits is mixed.

points.heading: Investment styles
points.text: Growth investors buy companies with fast-rising earnings, accepting high valuations. Value investors buy companies priced below intrinsic value. Quality, momentum and dividend-yield styles also exist. Styles go in and out of favour, which is why diversified portfolios mix them. No single style wins in every cycle.

formulas: P/E = Market price / EPS
Dividend yield = Dividend per share / Market price
Dividend discount model (constant growth): Price = D1 / (k - g)
traps: Thinking a bonus issue increases a shareholder's wealth - total value is unchanged; only the share count rises.
Comparing P/E ratios across unrelated industries such as banks and software companies.
Assuming a high dividend yield always signals a good investment; it may reflect a collapsing price.
Defining large caps by a fixed rupee threshold instead of rank (top 100).
items.recap: Equity returns = dividends + price change; earnings drive the long run. P/E = price / EPS; dividend yield = DPS / price; P/B suits banks. Bonus and split change share count, not value. Large cap = top 100, mid = 101-250. Fundamental analysis finds value; technical analysis times trades.

items.title: Bonds, Yields and Duration for NISM X-A: Revision Notes
items.description: Bond pricing, current yield, YTM, duration, convexity, credit ratings, zero-coupon bonds and debt market risks with worked examples for NISM X-A.
items.intro: Debt is a core building block of client portfolios, and X-A tests it with calculations and concepts. You must understand the inverse price-yield relationship, compute current yield and duration effects, and know the risks of debt instruments. Questions also test government versus corporate bonds and ratings.

points.heading: Bond basics
points.text: A bond pays periodic coupons and returns face value at maturity. An 8% bond with ₹100 face value pays ₹8 a year. The issuer may be the government, a PSU, a bank or a company. Secured bonds are backed by assets; debentures may be secured or unsecured.

points.heading: Price and yield move inversely
points.text: When market interest rates rise, existing fixed-coupon bonds become less attractive and their prices fall; when rates fall, prices rise. A long-maturity bond's price moves more than a short-maturity bond's for the same change in yield. A gilt fund can therefore post a loss in a rising rate year.

points.heading: Current yield and YTM
points.text: Current yield = annual coupon / price: an 8% coupon bond at ₹95 has a current yield of 8.42%. Yield to maturity also includes the gain or loss to maturity and assumes coupons are reinvested at the YTM. A bond below par has YTM above its coupon.

points.heading: Duration
points.text: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows. Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + yield). A bond with Macaulay duration of 6 years and YTM of 9% has modified duration of about 5.5, so a 50 basis point rise in yield cuts its price by about 2.75%.

points.heading: Convexity
points.text: Duration gives a straight-line estimate, but the real price-yield curve is convex. For normal bonds, convexity means prices rise more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount - a benefit to the holder. Higher convexity is valuable when rates are volatile.

points.heading: Credit risk and ratings
points.text: Credit rating agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings rate issuers' ability to pay. AAA is the highest; BBB- is the lowest investment grade. A downgrade raises the required yield and lowers the bond's price. Spreads over G-secs widen for lower ratings.

points.heading: Zero-coupon bonds
points.text: Zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value with no periodic coupons. Held to maturity, they eliminate reinvestment risk because there are no coupons to reinvest, but their duration equals maturity, so they are very sensitive to rate changes.

points.heading: Other debt risks
points.text: Reinvestment risk arises when coupons must be reinvested at lower rates; liquidity risk when bonds trade thinly; call risk when issuers redeem early after rates fall; inflation risk erodes fixed coupons. Floating-rate bonds reduce interest rate risk because coupons reset.

points.heading: Government and small savings
points.text: G-secs and state development loans carry sovereign backing. Small savings schemes - PPF, NSC, Senior Citizens Savings Scheme, Sukanya Samriddhi - have administered rates reset quarterly by the government. Check current rates on the official notifications. PPF also offers tax benefits under the old regime.

formulas: Current yield = Annual coupon / Market price
Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + YTM)
% Price change ≈ - Modified duration x Change in yield
traps: Saying bond prices rise when rates rise - the relationship is inverse.
Using Macaulay duration directly to estimate price change; convert to modified duration first.
Thinking zero-coupon bonds have low interest rate risk; their duration equals maturity, so it is high.
Treating current yield and YTM as identical; YTM includes the pull to par.
items.recap: Bond prices and yields move inversely; longer duration means bigger moves. Current yield = coupon / price; YTM adds pull to par. Modified duration = Macaulay / (1 + y); price change ≈ -MD x yield change. Convexity favours holders. Ratings drive credit spreads. Zero-coupon bonds remove reinvestment risk but carry high rate risk.

items.title: Derivatives for Investment Advisers: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Futures and options basics, payoffs, hedging a client portfolio with puts or futures and the risks of leverage - derivatives revision for NISM X-A.
items.intro: X-A does not expect trading expertise, but advisers must explain derivatives, recognise when they help a client and when they add risk. This chapter covers futures and options basics, payoffs and common hedging uses. Expect a payoff calculation and scenario questions about protecting a portfolio.

points.heading: What derivatives are
points.text: Derivatives are contracts whose value depends on an underlying asset such as shares, an index, currencies, commodities or interest rates. In India, equity derivatives trade on NSE and BSE under SEBI regulation; currency and interest rate derivatives involve RBI as well.

points.heading: Futures versus options buyer
points.text: A futures buyer is obliged to buy at the agreed price and faces unlimited gains or losses with daily mark-to-market. An option buyer pays a premium for the right, not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put); the maximum loss is the premium.

points.heading: Call option payoff
points.text: An investor buys a call with a strike of ₹500 for a ₹20 premium. If the stock is at ₹540 at expiry, the payoff is 540 - 500 - 20 = ₹20 per share. If it ends at or below ₹500, the call expires worthless and the loss is ₹20.

points.heading: Put option payoff
points.text: A put with strike ₹500 bought for ₹15 is profitable below the break-even of ₹485. If the stock falls to ₹450, profit is 500 - 450 - 15 = ₹35 per share. Puts act like insurance on holdings. Maximum profit is ₹485 if the price hits zero.

points.heading: Protecting a client's portfolio
points.text: A client with a diversified equity portfolio who fears a sharp fall but wants to keep upside can buy index put options. Selling index futures also hedges, but it removes upside as well. The put costs a premium, much like an insurance policy.

points.heading: Leverage and risk
points.text: Derivatives require only a margin, so small price moves create large gains or losses relative to capital. SEBI studies show most individual traders in equity F&O lose money. Advisers should be cautious about recommending derivatives for speculation to retail clients.

points.heading: Forwards and swaps
points.text: Forwards are customised OTC contracts often used by exporters and importers through banks to fix exchange rates. Interest rate swaps exchange fixed and floating payments and are used mainly by companies and banks to manage rate exposure. Retail clients rarely need these directly.

points.heading: Derivatives in products
points.text: Arbitrage funds use futures to lock in cash-futures spreads; some PMS and AIF strategies use options; market-linked debentures embed options. Advisers must understand the embedded derivative to explain how the product's payoff and risk really work. Market-linked debentures can be particularly complex to evaluate.

formulas: Call payoff = max(0, S - K) - premium
Put payoff = max(0, K - S) - premium
traps: Saying an option buyer must buy at expiry - the buyer has a right, the seller has the obligation.
Recommending futures selling when the client wants protection but also wants to keep upside - buying puts fits better.
Ignoring the premium when calculating option profit.
Treating derivative trading as a suitable income source for an inexperienced retail client.
items.recap: Derivatives derive value from an underlying. Futures carry obligations and linear payoffs; option buyers have rights and lose at most the premium. Call profit = S - K - premium; put profit = K - S - premium. Index puts protect a portfolio while keeping upside. Leverage magnifies losses; be cautious with retail clients.

items.title: Mutual Funds for Investment Advisers: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: NAV calculation, scheme categories, direct vs regular plans, equity-oriented tax test and choosing funds for client needs - NISM X-A revision notes.
items.intro: Mutual funds are the product advisers recommend most often, so X-A tests them in practical terms: NAV, categories, plans, costs, taxation and suitability. Questions are short scenarios - a client's need is described and you choose the category, or a number is given and you compute NAV.

points.heading: NAV calculation
points.text: NAV = (investments + other assets - liabilities) / units outstanding. A scheme with investments worth ₹120 crore, liabilities of ₹2 crore and 8 crore units has an NAV of ₹14.75. NAV is declared daily for open-ended schemes and already reflects expenses.

points.heading: Categories that matter
points.text: SEBI defines equity categories by market cap and style, debt categories by duration or credit quality, and hybrid categories by equity-debt mix. Advisers use categories to match risk and horizon rather than chasing individual scheme returns. Two funds in one category may still differ sharply in style and risk.

points.heading: Short-term parking
points.text: A client parking surplus cash for about two months with low risk and quick access is best served by a liquid or overnight fund, or a money market fund for slightly longer. Equity or long duration funds are unsuitable for such short horizons.

points.heading: Direct versus regular plans
points.text: A direct plan has no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower and NAV grows faster than the regular plan's over time. SEBI-registered investment advisers generally implement advice through direct plans, since they cannot receive commission from the same client.

points.heading: Tax classification
points.text: A scheme is 'equity-oriented' for tax purposes if it invests at least 65% in equity shares of domestic listed companies. Such schemes enjoy concessional long-term gains after 12 months. Funds with over 65% in debt bought after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates, as of 2026.

points.heading: Passive options
points.text: Index funds and ETFs offer market returns at low cost. For large cap exposure, many advisers prefer index funds because consistently beating the index after costs is difficult. Tracking error and expense ratio are the main comparison points. Large passive funds also have low turnover.

points.heading: Evaluating schemes
points.text: Compare a scheme with its benchmark TRI and category peers on rolling returns, risk-adjusted ratios, portfolio quality, expense ratio and fund manager consistency. A single year's top ranking says little about future results. Rolling three- and five-year returns reveal how consistently a fund has delivered.

points.heading: Systematic plans
points.text: SIPs build discipline and average purchase costs; STPs move a lump sum gradually from a liquid fund to equity; SWPs generate regular cash flow in retirement while the rest stays invested. Each SWP withdrawal is a redemption with tax on the gain portion only.

formulas: NAV = (Assets - Liabilities) / Units outstanding
traps: Recommending an equity fund for money needed in two months because recent returns were high.
Assuming the direct plan has a different portfolio from the regular plan; only expenses differ.
Using 50% instead of 65% domestic equity as the equity-oriented threshold.
Thinking an investment adviser can take commission on regular plans from the same advisory client.
items.recap: NAV = net assets / units. Pick categories by horizon and risk: liquid or overnight for short-term cash, equity for long goals. Direct plans cost less and suit advisory clients. Equity-oriented = 65%+ domestic equity. Prefer low-cost index funds where active managers struggle. Use SIP, STP and SWP to match cash flows.

items.title: Real Estate, Gold and Alternative Assets: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Real estate economics, REITs and InvITs, gold ETFs, sovereign gold bonds, and the role of alternative assets in client portfolios - NISM X-A notes.
items.intro: Indian households hold a large share of wealth in property and gold, so advisers must evaluate these assets objectively. This chapter covers direct real estate, REITs and InvITs, the forms of gold investment and other alternatives. Questions compare features such as liquidity, cost, income and regulation.

points.heading: Direct real estate
points.text: Property can provide rental income and appreciation, but it needs large lump sums, carries high transaction costs (stamp duty, registration, brokerage), is illiquid and concentrated in one location. Rental yields on Indian residential property are often modest compared with loan interest rates.

points.heading: Evaluating property returns
points.text: Total return includes rent net of maintenance, property tax and vacancies, plus price appreciation, minus transaction costs on purchase and sale. A flat bought for ₹80 lakh earning ₹20,000 a month in rent has a gross rental yield of 3%.

points.heading: REITs
points.text: Real Estate Investment Trusts, regulated by SEBI, own income-producing commercial property such as office parks and malls. They must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows to unit holders and invest mostly in completed, rent-generating assets. Units are listed and can be traded like shares.

points.heading: InvITs
points.text: Infrastructure Investment Trusts hold infrastructure assets like toll roads, power transmission lines and pipelines. Like REITs, they distribute most of their cash flows. Returns depend on traffic, tariffs and concession periods, so they carry asset-specific risks. Some InvITs are privately placed, not listed for retail.

points.heading: Forms of gold
points.text: Jewellery carries making charges and purity concerns. Gold ETFs and gold fund of funds track gold prices without storage issues. Sovereign Gold Bonds paid 2.5% annual interest and were tax-free on redemption at maturity for individuals, though fresh tranches depend on government issuance. Electronic Gold Receipts trade on exchanges.

points.heading: Role of gold
points.text: Gold tends to hold value during crises and when the rupee weakens, so it diversifies equity-heavy portfolios. It generates no income (except SGB interest), and returns can be flat for long stretches. Many advisers keep gold to around 5% to 15% of a portfolio.

points.heading: Other alternatives
points.text: Silver ETFs, international equity funds, commodities, art, collectibles, unlisted shares and peer-to-peer lending are other options. Many are illiquid, hard to value or lightly regulated. Advisers should assess them only for clients who understand and can bear the risks. Valuation and exit can be very difficult.

points.heading: Concentration in property
points.text: Many clients have most of their net worth in one or two properties. Advisers should point out the concentration and liquidity risk and avoid treating the self-occupied home as an asset available for retirement income unless the client plans to sell or rent it out.

formulas: Gross rental yield = Annual rent / Property value x 100
traps: Assuming REITs can invest mainly in under-construction projects - most assets must be completed and income-generating.
Forgetting the 90% minimum distribution requirement for REITs and InvITs.
Treating gold jewellery as an efficient investment despite making charges and purity issues.
Counting the client's self-occupied home as a liquid retirement asset.
items.recap: Direct property: big tickets, high costs, illiquid, modest rental yields. REITs (commercial property) and InvITs (infrastructure) are SEBI-regulated, listed and distribute at least 90% of cash flows. Gold diversifies and hedges crises; prefer ETFs, gold funds or SGBs over jewellery. Alternatives suit only informed clients.

items.title: PMS and AIF Rules for Advisers: NISM X-A Revision Notes
items.description: Minimum investment for PMS and AIFs, discretionary vs non-discretionary PMS, AIF categories, fees and suitability for HNI clients - NISM X-A notes.
items.intro: For wealthier clients, advisers must understand managed portfolios beyond mutual funds. This chapter covers Portfolio Management Services, Alternative Investment Funds and similar products: minimum ticket sizes, structures, fees and risks. Questions test the minimum investments, PMS types and AIF categories.

points.heading: PMS basics
points.text: A Portfolio Management Service manages a client's money in a separate account in the client's own name, regulated by SEBI's Portfolio Managers Regulations. SEBI requires a minimum investment of ₹50 lakh per client (check current limits). The client directly owns the securities in the portfolio.

points.heading: Types of PMS
points.text: In discretionary PMS, the manager decides what to buy and sell without seeking approval for each trade. In non-discretionary PMS, the manager advises and executes only with the client's consent. Advisory PMS only recommends; the client executes. Most retail-facing PMS offerings are discretionary.

points.heading: PMS fees and reporting
points.text: Fees can be fixed, performance-linked or both, often with a hurdle rate and high-water mark. Portfolio managers must disclose fees in the disclosure document and send periodic reports. Performance must be reported in the standardised format SEBI prescribes for comparability.

points.heading: AIF basics
points.text: Alternative Investment Funds pool money from sophisticated investors under SEBI's AIF Regulations. The general minimum investment is ₹1 crore per investor (₹25 lakh for employees or directors of the manager), with exemptions for accredited investors in certain schemes. Accredited investor status depends on income or net worth criteria.

points.heading: AIF categories
points.text: Category I invests in start-ups, SMEs, social ventures and infrastructure, which the government sees as beneficial. Category II includes private equity and private debt funds without leverage beyond operational needs. Category III uses complex strategies such as long-short and can use leverage.

points.heading: AIF structure and liquidity
points.text: AIFs are usually trusts with a sponsor and manager who must have skin in the game. Category I and II funds are closed-ended with tenures of several years; Category III can be open or closed-ended. Exit before maturity is limited.

points.heading: Comparing with mutual funds
points.text: PMS offers customisation and direct ownership but higher minimums and costs and less diversification. AIFs offer access to private markets but are illiquid. Mutual funds remain more liquid, cheaper and more tightly regulated for retail investors. Taxation also differs: PMS gains are taxed in the client's hands on every trade.

points.heading: Suitability checks
points.text: Only clients with adequate wealth, long horizons and a clear understanding of risks should consider PMS or AIFs. Advisers should check concentration, liquidity needs, fee drag and the manager's track record, and avoid recommending them just because a client is wealthy.

traps: Mixing up PMS (₹50 lakh minimum) and AIF (₹1 crore minimum) thresholds.
Describing non-discretionary PMS as one where the manager trades freely - that is discretionary.
Placing hedge-fund style leveraged strategies in Category I or II; they are Category III.
Assuming PMS securities are pooled like mutual fund units; they are held in the client's own name.
items.recap: PMS: separate account in client's name, ₹50 lakh minimum, discretionary or non-discretionary. AIF: pooled vehicle, ₹1 crore general minimum, Category I (socially beneficial), II (PE and debt), III (complex, leverage allowed). Both are less liquid and costlier than mutual funds; recommend only to suitable, informed clients.

items.title: Asset Allocation and Rebalancing: NISM X-A Revision Notes
items.description: Strategic vs tactical allocation, correlation and diversification, expected portfolio return, rebalancing back to target and core-satellite for NISM X-A.
items.intro: Asset allocation is the adviser's most powerful tool. This chapter covers how to set a client's mix of asset classes, how diversification works through correlation, how to compute portfolio expected return and how to rebalance. Expect calculations and comparisons of strategic, tactical and dynamic approaches.

points.heading: Why allocation matters
points.text: The mix of equity, debt, gold and cash explains most of the variation in a portfolio's long-term returns and risk. Choosing between two good large cap funds matters far less than deciding whether the client holds 30% or 70% in equity.

points.heading: Strategic asset allocation
points.text: Strategic allocation is the long-term target mix based on the client's goals, horizon and risk profile - for example 60% equity, 30% debt and 10% gold. It changes only when the client's circumstances change, such as approaching retirement. It is recorded in the investment policy statement.

points.heading: Tactical asset allocation
points.text: Tactical allocation makes temporary deviations from the strategic mix to exploit perceived market opportunities, such as raising equity by 5% after a sharp fall. It requires skill and discipline; mistimed moves can hurt returns. Limits on tactical shifts, such as plus or minus 10% from the strategic weight, keep the portfolio anchored to the client's risk profile.

points.heading: Correlation and diversification
points.text: Diversification reduces risk most when assets have low or negative correlation. Equity and gold have historically shown low correlation, so combining them smooths returns. Two highly correlated assets, such as two large cap funds, offer little diversification benefit. Correlations tend to rise during market crises.

points.heading: Expected portfolio return
points.text: Expected return is the weighted average of asset returns. With 60% equity at 12%, 30% debt at 7% and 10% gold at 8%, expected return = 7.2 + 2.1 + 0.8 = 10.1%. Portfolio risk, however, is lower than the weighted average of individual risks unless correlations are perfect.

points.heading: Rebalancing
points.text: If a 60:40 equity-debt portfolio drifts to 70:30 after a rally, rebalancing sells equity and buys debt to restore 60:40. This locks in gains and controls risk. Rebalancing can be calendar-based (yearly) or threshold-based (when drift exceeds, say, 5%). Tax and exit loads affect the choice of method.

points.heading: Life-stage and goal-based allocation
points.text: Young investors with long horizons can hold more equity; allocation shifts towards debt as goals approach. Goal-based allocation assigns separate buckets to each goal, so a house purchase in two years is in debt while retirement savings stay in equity.

points.heading: Core and satellite
points.text: A core-satellite approach puts most of the portfolio in low-cost diversified holdings such as index funds (the core) and a smaller part in active or thematic ideas (satellites). It balances cost control with the chance to add value. Satellites are usually capped at 20-30% of the portfolio.

formulas: Expected portfolio return = Sum of (weight x expected return) for each asset
Two-asset portfolio variance = w1²σ1² + w2²σ2² + 2w1w2ρσ1σ2
traps: Calling a short-term shift to exploit market conditions 'strategic' - that is tactical allocation.
Assuming diversification works best with highly correlated assets; low or negative correlation helps most.
Thinking portfolio risk is the simple weighted average of individual risks.
Letting a portfolio drift indefinitely after a rally instead of rebalancing to target.
items.recap: Allocation drives most outcomes. Strategic = long-term target; tactical = temporary tilts. Low correlation gives the most diversification. Expected return is a weighted average; risk is lower unless correlation is 1. Rebalance by calendar or threshold. Use goal buckets and a low-cost core with smaller satellites.

items.title: Sharpe, Treynor and Alpha: NISM X-A Performance Notes
items.description: Holding period return, CAGR, XIRR, Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha, Sortino and information ratio with worked numbers for NISM X-A revision.
items.intro: Advisers must report performance honestly and judge whether a portfolio or fund is adding value. This chapter covers return measures for different cash flow patterns and risk-adjusted ratios. Calculation questions are common: memorise the formulas and practise with the numbers below.

points.heading: Holding period return
points.text: HPR = (ending value - beginning value + income) / beginning value. A ₹1 lakh investment worth ₹1.12 lakh after a year with ₹2,000 of dividends gave a 14% HPR. It ignores the time taken, so annualise it for comparisons.

points.heading: CAGR and XIRR
points.text: CAGR suits a single lump sum: ₹1 lakh becoming ₹2 lakh in six years is about 12.2% a year. When there are multiple cash flows at different dates, such as SIPs, withdrawals and top-ups, XIRR gives the correct annualised return.

points.heading: Time-weighted vs money-weighted
points.text: Time-weighted return removes the effect of client deposits and withdrawals, so it measures the manager's skill. Money-weighted return (IRR or XIRR) reflects the client's actual experience, including the timing of their contributions. If a client adds a large sum just before a market fall, the money-weighted return will look much worse than the time-weighted return of the same fund.

points.heading: Sharpe ratio
points.text: Sharpe = (portfolio return - risk-free rate) / standard deviation. A fund returning 14% with SD 16% and a 6% risk-free rate has a Sharpe ratio of 0.5. It uses total risk, so it suits evaluating a client's whole portfolio.

points.heading: Treynor ratio
points.text: Treynor = (portfolio return - risk-free rate) / beta. A fund earning 13% with beta 1.4 and risk-free 6% has a Treynor ratio of 5. It uses only systematic risk, so it suits well-diversified portfolios that are part of a larger holding.

points.heading: Jensen's alpha
points.text: Alpha = actual return - [risk-free + beta x (market return - risk-free)]. A fund with beta 1.2 earning 15% when the market returned 12% and risk-free was 6% has expected return 6 + 1.2 x 6 = 13.2%, so alpha is 1.8%.

points.heading: Sortino and information ratio
points.text: Sortino ratio divides excess return by downside deviation only, so it does not penalise upside volatility. Information ratio = active return / tracking error, showing how consistently a manager beats the benchmark per unit of active risk. Higher values are better for both ratios.

points.heading: Benchmarks and attribution
points.text: Performance means little without a suitable benchmark: a blended benchmark for a 60:40 portfolio, or the TRI for an equity fund. Attribution analysis splits excess return into allocation effect and security selection effect. This tells the adviser whether outperformance came from choosing the right asset mix or from picking the right securities within each asset class.

formulas: Sharpe = (Rp - Rf) / σp
Treynor = (Rp - Rf) / βp
Jensen's alpha = Rp - [Rf + βp x (Rm - Rf)]
Information ratio = (Rp - Rb) / Tracking error
traps: Using Treynor for a concentrated, undiversified portfolio - Sharpe is more appropriate because unsystematic risk remains.
Using CAGR for a portfolio with many SIP contributions; XIRR is needed.
Forgetting to subtract the risk-free rate before dividing in Sharpe or Treynor.
Computing alpha as fund return minus market return, ignoring beta.
items.recap: HPR for one period; CAGR for lump sums; XIRR for multiple cash flows. Time-weighted judges the manager, money-weighted reflects the client. Sharpe uses SD, Treynor uses beta, alpha adjusts for beta, Sortino uses downside risk, information ratio uses tracking error. Always compare with a suitable benchmark.

items.title: Behavioural Finance Biases for Advisers: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Disposition effect, loss aversion, recency, herding, overconfidence, anchoring and mental accounting with Indian client examples for NISM X-A revision.
items.intro: Clients are not perfectly rational, and their biases often cost more than poor fund selection. This chapter covers the main behavioural biases, how they appear in client behaviour, and how advisers can counter them. Questions describe a client's action and ask you to name the bias.

points.heading: Why behaviour matters
points.text: Traditional finance assumes investors are rational and markets efficient. Behavioural finance shows that emotions and mental shortcuts lead to systematic errors - buying high, selling low and holding losers. An adviser's job includes protecting clients from their own reactions. Good process reduces such errors.

points.heading: Disposition effect
points.text: Investors tend to sell winners quickly to lock in gains but hold losers hoping to break even. A client who sells a stock up 20% but keeps one down 40% 'until it recovers' shows this bias, which is linked to loss aversion and regret avoidance.

points.heading: Loss aversion
points.text: Losses feel about twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good, according to prospect theory. This makes clients avoid equity altogether after one bad experience, or refuse to sell a loss-making investment even when the original reason for holding has disappeared.

points.heading: Recency and extrapolation
points.text: Recency bias gives too much weight to recent events. After a year of very high equity returns, a client may insist on sharply raising equity allocation because 'markets always go up', ignoring long-term averages and the risk of a correction.

points.heading: Herding
points.text: Herding means following the crowd - investing in a hot IPO, a popular theme or crypto because friends and social media are doing it. Herd behaviour feeds bubbles and crashes. Advisers should anchor decisions to the client's own plan. Many clients enter just before peaks.

points.heading: Overconfidence and illusion of control
points.text: Overconfident investors overestimate their knowledge and trade too much, increasing costs and taxes. Those with an illusion of control believe active monitoring improves outcomes. Both are common among successful professionals managing their own money. Frequent trading in a demat account and concentrated bets on familiar companies are typical signs that an adviser should discuss.

points.heading: Anchoring and mental accounting
points.text: Anchoring is fixating on a reference point, like a stock's past high or purchase price. Mental accounting treats money differently by source - spending a bonus freely while borrowing on a credit card at 36%. Both lead to inconsistent decisions.

points.heading: Countering biases
points.text: Written investment policies, goal-based buckets, automatic SIPs, scheduled rebalancing and pre-agreed rules for selling help clients avoid emotional decisions. Advisers should explain likely drawdowns in advance so clients are not surprised when they happen. Reviewing past decisions with the client, including the mistakes, builds better habits and trust over the long term.

traps: Confusing the disposition effect (sell winners, hold losers) with herding (following others).
Labelling a client who raises equity after a great year as 'overconfident' when the question points to recency bias.
Treating loss aversion as mere risk aversion; it is the asymmetric pain of losses versus gains.
Thinking advisers are immune to biases; they need processes too.
items.recap: Biases cost clients money. Disposition effect: sell winners, hold losers. Loss aversion: losses hurt about twice as much. Recency: extrapolating recent returns. Herding: following the crowd. Overconfidence: excessive trading. Anchoring and mental accounting distort decisions. Counter them with written plans, SIPs, rebalancing rules and expectation setting.

items.title: KYC, Demat and Transactions for Advisers: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: KYC Registration Agencies, CKYC, NSDL and CDSL, demat accounts, nomination, power of attorney rules and transaction processes - NISM X-A revision notes.
items.intro: Advisers must know the operational side of investing so clients can implement advice smoothly. This chapter covers KYC and the KRA system, demat accounts and depositories, nomination and the mechanics of buying and selling securities and funds. Questions are factual and procedural.

points.heading: KYC and KRAs
points.text: KYC verifies a client's identity and address and is mandatory under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. SEBI-registered KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) store KYC records centrally, so a client verified once by one intermediary need not repeat the full process with another.

points.heading: Central KYC
points.text: The CKYC Registry, managed by CERSAI, holds KYC records across sectors - banking, insurance, securities and pensions. Clients receive a 14-digit KYC Identification Number. Intermediaries upload and download records, reducing duplication. A client who completed KYC for a bank account can often use the same KIN when opening a demat account, saving time and paperwork.

points.heading: Documents and in-person verification
points.text: PAN is mandatory for securities market transactions. Proof of address and identity can be Aadhaar, passport, voter ID or driving licence. In-person verification can be done physically or through video. Aadhaar-based eKYC is widely used for online onboarding. KYC must be updated when details change.

points.heading: Depositories
points.text: India has two depositories, NSDL and CDSL, which hold securities in electronic form. Investors access them through depository participants such as banks and brokers. Dematerialisation removes risks of physical certificates such as forgery, loss and delays in transfer. Both are regulated by SEBI.

points.heading: Demat and trading accounts
points.text: A trading account with a broker is used to place orders; the demat account holds the securities. A linked bank account handles funds. Shares bought are credited to the demat account after settlement; sold shares are debited through a delivery instruction or eDIS authorisation.

points.heading: Nomination
points.text: Investors are encouraged to nominate in demat accounts and mutual fund folios or explicitly opt out. Nomination ensures quick transmission to the nominee on death. SEBI has expanded nomination facilities - check the current maximum number of nominees. Without it, legal heirs face lengthy paperwork.

points.heading: Power of attorney limits
points.text: SEBI has restricted the use of broad powers of attorney. Brokers now use the Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction (DDPI) for specific purposes such as settling sales and margin pledges, rather than open-ended control over a client's account. This protects client securities from misuse.

points.heading: Mutual fund transactions
points.text: Mutual fund units can be held in statement form or in demat. Transactions happen through AMC websites, RTAs, MF Central, exchange platforms or advisers' execution tools. Advisers should implement through direct plans and keep records of client consent. Clients should transact only in their own name.

traps: Naming CDSL and NSE as India's depositories - NSDL and CDSL are the depositories; NSE is an exchange.
Confusing a KRA (securities market KYC) with the CKYC Registry (cross-sector, run by CERSAI).
Assuming the trading account holds shares; the demat account does.
Thinking brokers may still take an unrestricted power of attorney; DDPI limits use to specific purposes.
items.recap: KYC is mandatory under PMLA; KRAs store securities KYC, CKYC (CERSAI) works across sectors. PAN is mandatory. NSDL and CDSL are the depositories, accessed via DPs. Trading account places orders, demat account holds securities. Nominate or opt out. DDPI replaced broad powers of attorney. Implement advice through direct plans with documented consent.

items.title: SEBI Investment Adviser Regulations: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: SEBI IA Regulations on registration, qualifications, fees, risk profiling, suitability, segregation from distribution and exemptions - NISM X-A notes.
items.intro: This chapter covers the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 and their amendments - who must register, qualification and certification requirements, fee rules, and the obligations on suitability and documentation. It is heavily tested. Several limits have been revised recently, so verify current numbers with SEBI as of 2026.

points.heading: Who must register
points.text: Anyone giving investment advice for consideration, directly or indirectly, must register with SEBI as an investment adviser unless exempt. This includes individuals, partnerships and companies. Using titles like 'financial planner' or 'wealth adviser' while advising for a fee without registration is a violation.

points.heading: Exemptions
points.text: Exempt categories include persons giving incidental advice in their main profession - such as lawyers, chartered accountants and company secretaries - and mutual fund distributors or brokers giving incidental advice on products they sell. Insurance agents under IRDAI and pension advisers under PFRDA are also exempt for those products.

points.heading: Qualification and certification
points.text: Individual advisers and principal officers need educational qualifications and NISM certifications (Series X-A and X-B, or the consolidated requirement prescribed by SEBI), and must keep them current through renewal. Persons associated with advice need the same certification. Lapsed certification can bar an adviser from practising.

points.heading: Supervision by BASL
points.text: SEBI has recognised BSE Administration and Supervision Ltd (BASL) as the body that administers and supervises investment advisers, including enrolment, fee collection and periodic inspection. Advisers must be members of BASL in addition to being registered with SEBI. Its inspections complement SEBI's own oversight.

points.heading: Remuneration
points.text: An adviser may receive fees only from the client, never commissions from product providers on the same client. SEBI caps fees for individual and HUF clients through a fixed-fee limit per family or a percentage of assets under advice, and limits how far in advance fees can be collected. Check current limits on SEBI's website.

points.heading: Segregation from distribution
points.text: Advisory and distribution activities must be kept separate at the client level: a client who takes advice cannot be sold products for commission by the same adviser or its group. Individual advisers cannot act as distributors at all. Family-level checks apply to related accounts.

points.heading: Risk profiling and suitability
points.text: Before advising, the adviser must profile the client's risk, document it and ensure every recommendation is suitable for that profile and the client's objectives. Where the client wants a product inconsistent with the profile, the adviser must record the deviation and the client's acknowledgement.

points.heading: Agreement and records
points.text: A written agreement covering scope, fees and terms must be signed before advice begins. Advisers must maintain records of client data, risk profiles, advice given and its rationale for at least five years, and conduct an annual compliance audit. Advice given over phone must be recorded.

traps: Assuming an IA may take commission as long as it is disclosed - advisers may receive fees only from clients.
Thinking all mutual fund distributors must register as IAs; incidental advice on their own products is exempt.
Forgetting the risk profiling and suitability documentation required before advice.
Quoting older fee caps as current - SEBI revised limits; check the latest circulars.
items.recap: Advice for consideration requires SEBI IA registration unless exempt (lawyers, CAs, distributors giving incidental advice). Advisers need NISM certification and BASL membership. Fees come only from clients, within SEBI caps. Advice and distribution are segregated at client level. Risk profiling, suitability, written agreements and five-year records are mandatory.

items.title: Adviser Ethics, Conflicts and Complaints: NISM X-A Notes
items.description: Fiduciary duty, conflict of interest disclosure, code of conduct, SCORES, SMART ODR and handling client complaints - ethics revision for NISM X-A.
items.intro: The last X-A chapter is about professional behaviour: putting the client first, managing conflicts of interest, and handling complaints properly. Questions present ethical dilemmas and ask for the correct course of action, or test the grievance escalation path.

points.heading: Fiduciary duty
points.text: Investment advisers act in a fiduciary capacity: they must place the client's interests above their own, act honestly and fairly, and exercise due skill and care. This is a higher standard than the suitability obligation of a product seller. The duty applies throughout the relationship.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: SEBI's code for advisers requires honesty, fairness, diligence, capability, adequate disclosure, confidentiality and compliance. Advisers must not make exaggerated claims, promise returns or misrepresent their qualifications or registration. They must also maintain adequate infrastructure, keep their knowledge up to date and ensure that any employee or representative follows the same standards when dealing with clients.

points.heading: Identifying conflicts
points.text: Conflicts arise whenever the adviser or a related person could benefit from a recommendation - for example, recommending a scheme managed by a spouse, a company in which the adviser holds shares, or a product from a group company. Such links must be disclosed upfront.

points.heading: Managing conflicts
points.text: When an adviser is about to recommend a scheme whose fund manager is her spouse, she must disclose the relationship to the client before advising and ensure the advice is still in the client's interest; if the conflict cannot be managed, she should avoid the recommendation.

points.heading: Personal trading
points.text: Advisers should not trade ahead of client recommendations (front-running) or against the advice they give. Many firms maintain restricted lists and pre-clearance processes. Personal holdings in recommended securities must be disclosed. Advisers should also avoid recommending securities they plan to sell from their own holdings, since the client's purchase could support the price at which they exit.

points.heading: Confidentiality
points.text: Client information must be kept confidential and used only for the advisory relationship, except where disclosure is required by law. Sharing client data with distributors or product providers without consent breaches the code. Data security also covers digital records, so advisers must protect client files, emails and passwords against leaks or unauthorised access by staff.

points.heading: Complaint redressal
points.text: An adviser must have a grievance mechanism and resolve complaints promptly, within SEBI's timelines. If the investor is not satisfied, the complaint can be lodged with SEBI on SCORES. Unresolved disputes can then go to the SMART ODR platform for online conciliation and arbitration.

points.heading: Disclosure of complaints
points.text: Advisers must display the status of complaints received and resolved on their websites in the format SEBI prescribes. This transparency helps prospective clients judge an adviser's service record. The data includes complaints pending at the start of the month, received, resolved and pending at month end, along with average resolution time.

traps: Thinking disclosure alone always cures a conflict - the advice must still be in the client's best interest.
Escalating directly to SMART ODR without first approaching the adviser and SCORES.
Assuming advisers can share client data with group companies freely; consent is required.
Treating the fiduciary standard as the same as product suitability; it is higher.
items.recap: Advisers are fiduciaries: client first, honesty, care and confidentiality. Identify conflicts such as family links or personal holdings, disclose them, and avoid advice that does not serve the client. No front-running. Complaints: adviser first, then SEBI SCORES, then SMART ODR. Publish complaint status as SEBI requires.

items.title: Currency Market Basics: NISM Series I Revision Notes
items.description: Base and quote currency, direct and indirect quotes, bid-ask spread, cross rates, spot settlement and India's exchange rate regime for NISM Series I.
items.intro: The first chapter of NISM Series I builds the vocabulary of foreign exchange: how currency pairs are quoted, how banks make two-way prices, how cross rates are derived and how India's exchange rate regime evolved. Questions are a mix of definitions and quick calculations, so practise reading quotes carefully.

points.heading: Base and quote currency
points.text: In the quote USD/INR = 84.10, USD is the base currency and INR is the quote (or price) currency: one US dollar costs ₹84.10. If the quote rises to 84.50, the dollar has appreciated and the rupee has depreciated. Always identify which currency is being priced before interpreting a move.

points.heading: Direct and indirect quotes
points.text: A direct quote states the price of one unit of foreign currency in domestic currency, such as EUR/INR = 91.20 for an Indian resident. An indirect quote states how much foreign currency one unit of domestic currency buys, such as 1 INR = 0.01096 EUR. India uses direct quotes in practice.

points.heading: Bid, ask and spread
points.text: A bank quoting USD/INR 83.40/83.45 buys dollars at 83.40 (bid) and sells at 83.45 (ask). A customer buying dollars pays the higher ask; one selling dollars receives the lower bid. The 5 paise spread is the dealer's margin and widens in volatile or illiquid conditions.

points.heading: Cross rates
points.text: A cross rate is derived from two quotes involving a common currency. If EUR/USD is 1.1000 and USD/INR is 84.00, EUR/INR = 1.10 x 84.00 = 92.40. Cross rates let traders price pairs that are not directly quoted and spot arbitrage when quotes are inconsistent.

points.heading: Settlement dates
points.text: A spot deal settles two business days after the trade date (T+2). Cash or value-today deals settle the same day; tom or value-tomorrow deals settle the next business day. Any settlement beyond spot is a forward. Holidays in either currency's centre push settlement out.

points.heading: Market structure
points.text: The global forex market is decentralised and OTC, run mainly by large banks across time zones, with the US dollar on one side of most trades. In India, authorised dealer banks quote to customers, the interbank market sets rates, and exchanges offer standardised currency futures and options.

points.heading: Exchange rate regimes
points.text: Under a fixed regime the central bank pegs the currency; under a free float, markets set the rate. India moved from a basket peg to the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System in 1992 and a unified market-determined rate in 1993. Today the rupee is a managed float, with RBI intervening to curb volatility.

points.heading: Convertibility
points.text: The rupee became fully convertible on the current account in 1994, meaning trade, travel and remittance payments are freely allowed. The capital account remains partially convertible, with limits on overseas investment by residents and on foreign borrowing, managed by RBI under FEMA.

points.heading: What drives exchange rates
points.text: Inflation differentials, interest rate differentials, current account balance, capital flows such as FPI investment, crude oil prices and global risk sentiment all influence USD/INR. A rise in crude prices widens India's import bill and tends to weaken the rupee. RBI intervention can smooth these moves.

formulas: Cross rate A/C = A/B x B/C (e.g. EUR/INR = EUR/USD x USD/INR)
Spread = Ask - Bid
traps: Mixing up base and quote currency - in USD/INR, USD is the base; the number is rupees per dollar.
Thinking a customer buying dollars pays the bid; customers pay the higher ask.
Assuming spot settlement is the same day - spot is T+2; same-day is 'cash'.
Saying a rise in USD/INR means the rupee strengthened; it means the rupee weakened.
items.recap: In USD/INR, USD is base, INR is quote. India uses direct quotes. Customers buy at ask, sell at bid. Cross rates multiply through a common currency. Spot = T+2, tom = T+1, cash = T+0. The rupee is a managed float, current-account convertible since 1994, capital account partly convertible.

items.title: Forex Forwards, Swaps and Parity: NISM Series I Notes
items.description: OTC currency forwards, futures vs forwards, interest rate parity, forward premium and discount, currency swaps and hedging exposures for NISM Series I.
items.intro: This chapter introduces the family of foreign exchange derivatives - forwards, futures, options and swaps - and the pricing principle that ties forward rates to interest rates. Questions test interest rate parity calculations, forward premiums, the distinctions between OTC and exchange-traded contracts, and who hedges what.

points.heading: Why hedge currency risk
points.text: Exporters lose when the rupee strengthens before they convert their dollar receipts; importers lose when it weakens before they pay. Students paying overseas fees and companies with foreign loans face similar risks. Derivatives let them lock in or cap the exchange rate.

points.heading: OTC forwards
points.text: A forward contract with a bank fixes the exchange rate for a future date and is customised in amount and maturity. Forwards carry counterparty risk and usually need an underlying exposure under RBI rules. They are the most widely used hedging tool for Indian corporates.

points.heading: Futures versus forwards
points.text: Exchange-traded currency futures are standardised in lot size and expiry, guaranteed by a clearing corporation, marked to market daily and accessible to smaller participants. Forwards are bilateral, customised and settled only at maturity, without daily margin. Futures are also more transparent on price.

points.heading: Interest rate parity
points.text: Forward rates reflect interest rate differentials. With USD/INR spot at 84.00, a one-year INR rate of 7% and USD rate of 4%, the one-year forward = 84 x 1.07 / 1.04 = 86.42. If the market forward differs, covered interest arbitrage would push it back.

points.heading: Forward premium and discount
points.text: The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount, and the lower-rate currency at a forward premium. Because Indian rates are usually higher than US rates, the dollar normally trades at a forward premium against the rupee.

points.heading: Currency swaps
points.text: In a cross-currency swap, two parties exchange principal in two currencies at the start, pay each other interest in the respective currencies during the term and re-exchange principal at maturity. Companies with foreign currency loans use swaps to convert them into rupee liabilities.

points.heading: Currency options
points.text: Options give the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell a currency at a strike rate. They protect against adverse moves while letting the hedger benefit from favourable moves, in exchange for an upfront premium - like insurance on the exchange rate.

points.heading: Hedging example
points.text: An exporter expecting USD receivables in three months sells USD/INR futures today. If the rupee strengthens, the lower rupee value of the receivables is offset by gains on the short futures. If the rupee weakens, the futures lose but the receivables are worth more, so the net rate is locked.

formulas: Forward rate = Spot x (1 + r domestic x t) / (1 + r foreign x t)
Annualised forward premium % = (Forward - Spot) / Spot x 12 / months x 100
traps: Assuming the higher-interest currency trades at a forward premium - it trades at a discount.
Treating a forward as exchange-traded with daily margins; that describes futures.
Thinking a hedger is speculating - an exporter selling futures against receivables reduces risk.
Forgetting that hedging locks the rate both ways, giving up gains from favourable moves (unless options are used).
items.recap: Forwards are custom OTC hedges; futures are standardised, cleared and marked to market. Interest rate parity: forward = spot x (1 + r_d) / (1 + r_f). Higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount, so USD usually stands at a premium to INR. Swaps exchange principal and interest across currencies. Options hedge while keeping upside.

items.title: USD/INR Futures Contract Specs: NISM Series I Notes
items.description: Lot size, tick size, expiry, final settlement price, MTM, basis and hedging with USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR futures for NISM Series I.
items.intro: This is the heaviest chapter in Series I. You must know contract specifications for USD/INR and other rupee pairs, how futures are settled, how to compute MTM and basis, and how importers and exporters hedge. Specifications are revised occasionally, so confirm current details on NSE and BSE websites as of 2026.

points.heading: Currency pairs traded
points.text: Indian exchanges offer futures on USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR, plus cross-currency pairs such as EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY. USD/INR is by far the most liquid contract, and volumes are concentrated in the near-month expiry. Cross-currency contracts are quoted in the second currency of the pair, such as US dollars per euro for EUR/USD.

points.heading: Contract size and quotation
points.text: The USD/INR futures lot is USD 1,000, and EUR/INR and GBP/INR lots are 1,000 units of the foreign currency. JPY/INR is quoted in rupees per 100 yen, with a lot of 1,00,000 yen. Prices are quoted to four decimal places in rupees.

points.heading: Tick size
points.text: The minimum price movement for rupee-pair futures is ₹0.0025, or a quarter of a paisa. On one USD/INR lot of USD 1,000, one tick is worth ₹2.50. Traders compute gains as ticks moved x tick value x number of lots.

points.heading: Expiry and last trading day
points.text: Monthly contracts are available for up to 12 months. The last trading day is two working days before the last business day of the expiry month, and final settlement happens on the last business day. Trading on expiry day stops earlier than normal hours.

points.heading: Cash settlement in rupees
points.text: USD/INR futures are cash settled in Indian rupees - no dollars change hands. The final settlement price is the RBI reference rate (published through FBIL) on the last trading day. Profits and losses are paid in rupees through the clearing corporation.

points.heading: Daily mark-to-market
points.text: A trader buys 10 USD/INR lots at 83.20 and the settlement price that day is 83.45. MTM profit = (83.45 - 83.20) x 1,000 x 10 = ₹2,500, credited the next day. The next day's MTM is computed from 83.45.

points.heading: Basis
points.text: Basis = spot - futures. With spot at 83.50 and near-month futures at 83.80, basis is -0.30. The futures premium reflects the interest rate differential and shrinks as expiry approaches, converging to the spot rate at final settlement. A wider gap means higher carry.

points.heading: Importer hedge
points.text: An importer who must pay USD 50,000 in two months fears rupee depreciation. Buying 50 lots of USD/INR futures locks in the rate: if the dollar rises, futures gains offset the higher rupee cost of the payment. If the dollar falls, the futures lose but the payment becomes cheaper.

points.heading: Exporter hedge outcome
points.text: An exporter sells USD/INR futures at 84.00. At expiry they settle at 85.00 and he sells his dollars in the spot market at 85.00. He loses ₹1 per dollar on futures but gains ₹1 versus 84.00 in spot, so his effective rate stays 84.00, ignoring basis and costs.

formulas: Futures P&L = (Exit price - Entry price) x Lot size x Number of lots (long)
Tick value = Tick size x Lot size = 0.0025 x 1,000 = ₹2.50 for USD/INR
Basis = Spot - Futures
traps: Quoting JPY/INR per one yen - it is quoted per 100 yen.
Assuming USD/INR futures are settled by delivery of dollars; they are cash settled in rupees.
Taking the last trading day as the last business day of the month - it is two working days earlier.
Hedging an importer's payable by selling futures; importers buy USD/INR futures.
items.recap: USD/INR lot USD 1,000, tick ₹0.0025, monthly expiries up to 12 months, last trading day two working days before month-end, cash settled in rupees at the RBI/FBIL reference rate. JPY/INR is per 100 yen. MTM daily. Basis = spot - futures, converging at expiry. Importers buy, exporters sell.

items.title: USD/INR Options, Premium and Greeks: NISM Series I
items.description: European-style USD/INR options, call and put payoffs, break-even, moneyness, intrinsic and time value, delta and margin rules for NISM Series I revision.
items.intro: Currency options are tested with many small calculations. You must know the contract features of USD/INR options on Indian exchanges, compute payoffs and break-evens on a per-lot basis, identify moneyness and split premium into intrinsic and time value. A few questions also cover Greeks and margins.

points.heading: Contract features
points.text: USD/INR options on Indian exchanges are European style, exercisable only on expiry, premium-settled in rupees and cash settled at the RBI/FBIL reference rate. The lot is USD 1,000. Options on EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR are also listed, along with weekly USD/INR expiries.

points.heading: Call payoff per lot
points.text: A trader buys one USD/INR 84.00 call for ₹0.30. If settlement is 84.60, payoff = (84.60 - 84.00 - 0.30) x 1,000 = ₹300 profit. If settlement is at or below 84.00, the call expires worthless and the loss is the ₹300 premium. Break-even is 84.30.

points.heading: Put payoff
points.text: Buying an 83.50 put for ₹0.20 gives a break-even of 83.30 (strike minus premium). If the rupee strengthens and USD/INR settles at 83.00, profit is (83.50 - 83.00 - 0.20) x 1,000 = ₹300. Above 83.50, the put lapses. Maximum loss is the ₹200 premium.

points.heading: Buyer and seller risk
points.text: The buyer of a currency call or put can lose at most the premium. The seller receives the premium but faces large losses if the rate moves against them, which is why sellers must deposit margin with the clearing corporation while buyers pay only the premium.

points.heading: Moneyness
points.text: For a call, spot above strike means in-the-money; for a put, spot below strike. With USD/INR spot at 84.20, an 84.50 put is in-the-money by 0.30 and an 84.50 call is out-of-the-money. At-the-money options have strike close to spot. Only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.

points.heading: Intrinsic and time value
points.text: A USD/INR 83.00 call trading at ₹1.40 with spot at 84.00 has intrinsic value 1.00 and time value 0.40. Time value reflects the chance of further favourable moves and decays to zero at expiry. An out-of-the-money option, such as an 85.00 call with spot at 84.00, has zero intrinsic value, so its whole premium is time value.

points.heading: What moves premiums
points.text: Premiums rise with higher volatility and longer time to expiry. A higher spot raises call premiums and lowers put premiums. The interest rate differential between INR and USD also affects premiums through the forward rate, as in the Garman-Kohlhagen model, a currency version of Black-Scholes.

points.heading: Delta and other Greeks
points.text: Delta measures the change in premium for a small change in the underlying exchange rate; an at-the-money call has delta around 0.5. Gamma measures the change in delta, theta the time decay, vega sensitivity to volatility, and rho to interest rates.

points.heading: Hedging with options
points.text: An importer worried about a weaker rupee can buy USD/INR calls to cap the cost of dollars while benefiting if the rupee strengthens. An exporter can buy puts to set a floor on receivable value. The premium is the cost of keeping upside.

formulas: Call break-even = Strike + Premium; Put break-even = Strike - Premium
Option P&L per lot = Payoff per USD x 1,000
Time value = Premium - Intrinsic value
traps: Treating USD/INR options as American style - they are European, exercisable only at expiry.
Saying option buyers must post margin; only sellers do, buyers pay premium.
Calling a put in-the-money when spot is above strike - for puts, spot must be below strike.
Forgetting to multiply by the USD 1,000 lot when asked for rupee profit.
items.recap: USD/INR options: European, lot USD 1,000, premium in rupees, cash settled at the reference rate. Call break-even = strike + premium; put = strike - premium. Buyers risk only premium; sellers post margin. Premium = intrinsic + time value. Volatility and time raise premiums. Importers buy calls, exporters buy puts.

items.title: Currency Futures and Options Strategies: NISM Series I
items.description: Bull spreads, straddles, calendar spreads, arbitrage and hedging strategies for exporters and importers using USD/INR derivatives - NISM Series I notes.
items.intro: This chapter applies futures and options to trading and hedging situations. Expect several calculations: maximum profit and loss of spreads, break-evens of straddles, and identifying arbitrage. Questions also ask which strategy matches a stated view - moderately bullish, unsure of direction, or hedging with upside.

points.heading: Bull call spread
points.text: A trader expecting USD/INR to rise moderately buys an 84.00 call at ₹0.50 and sells an 85.00 call at ₹0.15. Net cost is ₹0.35. Maximum profit = (1.00 - 0.35) x 1,000 = ₹650 above 85.00; maximum loss = ₹350 below 84.00; break-even 84.35.

points.heading: Bear put spread
points.text: To profit from a moderate rupee appreciation, buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put. Both profit and loss are capped. The sold put reduces the cost of protection but gives up gains beyond the lower strike. Maximum profit is the strike difference minus net premium.

points.heading: Long straddle
points.text: Ahead of a big policy announcement, a trader unsure of direction buys an 84.00 call at ₹0.40 and an 84.00 put at ₹0.35. Total premium is ₹0.75, so break-evens are 83.25 and 84.75. Profit comes only if USD/INR moves beyond either point.

points.heading: Long strangle
points.text: A strangle buys an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put, for example an 84.50 call and an 83.50 put. It costs less than a straddle but needs a larger move to profit. Short straddles and strangles profit in calm markets but risk large losses.

points.heading: Calendar spread
points.text: Selling a near-month USD/INR future and buying a far-month future (or vice versa) is a calendar spread. It profits from changes in the gap between the two contracts, which mainly reflects interest rate differentials, not the direction of the rupee. Margins are lower than for outright positions.

points.heading: Cash and futures arbitrage
points.text: If USD/INR futures trade well above their interest-parity fair value, an arbitrageur borrows rupees, buys dollars in spot (or OTC) and sells futures, locking in a riskless spread. Such activity pulls futures back to fair value. When futures are below fair value, the reverse trade applies.

points.heading: Hedging with protection and upside
points.text: An exporter wanting protection against rupee appreciation but still wanting to gain if the rupee depreciates should buy USD/INR put options. Selling futures would lock the rate but give up the upside; the put costs premium but keeps the benefit.

points.heading: Range forwards and collars
points.text: Buying a put and selling a call (for an exporter) creates a collar: the receivable's value is kept within a band, and the call premium received offsets the put premium. Zero-cost collars are popular but cap the upside. Importers build the mirror image: buy a call, sell a put.

formulas: Bull call spread max profit = (Higher strike - Lower strike - Net premium) x Lot
Straddle break-evens = Strike +/- (Call premium + Put premium)
traps: Calling a near-sell, far-buy futures position a directional trade - it is a calendar spread.
Choosing futures when the hedger wants protection plus upside; options are needed.
Using only one premium when computing straddle break-evens - add both.
Forgetting that a bull call spread's maximum profit is capped at the higher strike.
items.recap: Bull call spread: buy low strike, sell high strike, profit and loss capped. Straddles and strangles bet on big moves; break-evens use total premium. Calendar spreads trade the gap between expiries. Arbitrage sells overpriced futures against spot. Exporters wanting upside buy puts; collars cap both sides.

items.title: Currency Derivatives Trading Mechanism: NISM Series I
items.description: Trading hours, order types, members, UCC registration, position limits and the trading workflow in exchange-traded currency derivatives for NISM Series I.
items.intro: This chapter explains how currency derivatives are traded on Indian exchanges: the participants, the electronic trading system, order types and the rules for client identification and positions. Questions are factual, often about how a specific order type behaves or which member does what.

points.heading: Trading platforms
points.text: NSE, BSE and MSE run currency derivatives segments with anonymous, screen-based order matching on price-time priority. Trading hours for currency derivatives typically run from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm on weekdays, with earlier cut-offs on expiry for maturing contracts. Check the exchange for current timings.

points.heading: Member types
points.text: Trading members execute trades for themselves and clients. Clearing members clear and settle trades. Self-clearing members clear only their own trades. Professional Clearing Members, typically banks or custodians, clear and settle trades executed by other trading members but do not trade.

points.heading: Limit and market orders
points.text: A limit order to buy USD/INR futures at 83.50 executes only at 83.50 or lower. A market order executes immediately at the best available price, with the risk of slippage in thin markets. A limit order gives price certainty but may not execute at all, while a market order gives execution certainty but not price certainty.

points.heading: Stop-loss orders
points.text: A stop-loss sell order with a trigger of 83.20 becomes active only when the market trades at or below 83.20. It then becomes a limit or market order. Stop-losses help traders cap losses without watching screens continuously. A gap in prices can cause execution below the trigger.

points.heading: Order conditions
points.text: Day orders lapse at the end of the trading day if unexecuted. Immediate or Cancel orders execute at once, fully or partly, and cancel the rest. Orders must stay within the exchange's operating price range to prevent erroneous trades. Unexecuted orders do not carry over to the next day.

points.heading: Client registration
points.text: Before placing orders for a client, a trading member must complete KYC, register the client with the exchange under a Unique Client Code with PAN, and provide the Risk Disclosure Document and the rights and obligations document. Orders without a valid UCC are rejected.

points.heading: Position limits
points.text: Exchanges and SEBI set position limits at client, trading member and bank level, typically linked to a share of total open interest or a fixed dollar amount, whichever is higher. These limits prevent concentration and manipulation. Limits differ for each currency pair.

points.heading: RBI's exposure requirement
points.text: RBI's rules on exchange-traded currency derivatives require users to have an underlying exposure to currency risk, whether contracted or anticipated. Users may take positions up to a specified limit without producing documents, but must still have the exposure. Check the current RBI directions.

traps: Thinking a Professional Clearing Member can trade for its own book - it only clears for trading members.
Believing a stop-loss order executes at once; it waits for the trigger price.
Assuming anyone can trade currency derivatives purely to speculate under RBI's current rules - an underlying exposure is expected.
Forgetting that orders without a registered UCC are rejected.
items.recap: Currency derivatives trade on NSE, BSE and MSE with price-time priority. Trading members trade; clearing members settle; PCMs only clear for others. Limit, market, stop-loss, day and IOC orders behave differently. UCC with PAN and the RDD are required before trading. Position limits apply; RBI expects users to have underlying exposure.

items.title: Currency Derivatives Clearing and Margins: NISM Series I
items.description: Novation, SPAN initial margin, extreme loss margin, calendar spread margin, daily MTM, final settlement and the Settlement Guarantee Fund for NISM Series I.
items.intro: This chapter explains how the clearing corporation guarantees currency derivative trades and contains risk. Questions test novation, margin types and their purpose, the timing of MTM settlement, the Settlement Guarantee Fund and why spreads get lower margins.

points.heading: Novation
points.text: When a trade is matched, the clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. This replaces counterparty risk between members with the credit of the clearing corporation, which is backed by margins and default funds.

points.heading: Initial margin
points.text: Initial margin is collected upfront to cover the potential loss on a position over a day under adverse conditions. It is computed using SPAN with a high confidence level. For currency futures it is a small percentage of contract value, so leverage is high.

points.heading: Extreme loss margin
points.text: Extreme loss margin is charged in addition to initial margin to cover tail risks beyond SPAN's scenarios, usually as a percentage of the gross open position's value. Both margins must be in place before trading. It protects against sudden, unusually large swings in the exchange rate.

points.heading: Calendar spread margin
points.text: A long near-month and short far-month position in the same pair carries much less risk because both legs move together with the spot rate. Clearing corporations therefore charge a reduced calendar spread margin instead of full margins on both legs, as long as the near leg is not about to expire.

points.heading: Daily MTM settlement
points.text: Futures positions are marked to the daily settlement price, and profits and losses are settled in cash on T+1. Members collect MTM losses from clients and pass on gains. Failure to pay MTM can lead to positions being closed out.

points.heading: Final settlement
points.text: On expiry, open futures are settled in rupees against the final settlement price (the reference rate). In-the-money options are automatically exercised and cash settled. There is no physical delivery of foreign currency in rupee-pair contracts. Positions closed before expiry settle only through MTM and need no final settlement.

points.heading: Settlement Guarantee Fund
points.text: The Core Settlement Guarantee Fund ensures that settlement is completed even if a clearing member defaults. It is funded by contributions from the clearing corporation, the exchange and clearing members, and is used only after the defaulter's own margins are exhausted.

points.heading: Other risk controls
points.text: Clearing corporations monitor positions and margins in real time, enforce position limits, apply penalties for margin shortfalls and require members to segregate client collateral. Members that breach limits may have their trading terminals disabled. Clients are also expected to keep adequate margins at all times to avoid forced square-offs.

traps: Thinking novation transfers default risk to the other trading member - it moves it to the clearing corporation.
Assuming MTM is settled only at expiry; it is settled daily.
Confusing the Settlement Guarantee Fund (backs settlement) with the Investor Protection Fund (compensates clients of defaulting brokers).
Believing calendar spreads need full margin on both legs; they get a reduced spread margin.
items.recap: Novation makes the clearing corporation the counterparty. Initial margin via SPAN plus extreme loss margin, collected upfront. MTM in cash on T+1. Final settlement in rupees at the reference rate; no delivery. Spreads get lower margin. The Core SGF completes settlement if a member defaults.

items.title: Currency Derivatives Regulation in India: NISM Series I
items.description: Joint SEBI and RBI oversight, FEMA, SCRA, exchange eligibility, participant rules and the RBI exposure framework for currency derivatives - NISM Series I.
items.intro: Currency derivatives sit between two regulators: RBI, which governs foreign exchange, and SEBI, which governs exchanges. This chapter explains the legal basis, who regulates what and who may participate. Questions are few but predictable, mostly about regulatory roles and the laws involved.

points.heading: Joint regulation
points.text: Exchange-traded currency derivatives fall under the joint purview of RBI and SEBI. RBI decides the products and participant eligibility because they involve foreign exchange; SEBI regulates the exchanges, clearing corporations, members and trading practices. A joint RBI-SEBI standing technical committee coordinates policy.

points.heading: Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
points.text: RBI's authority over who can participate in currency derivatives and on what terms flows from FEMA, which replaced the older FERA in 2000. FEMA governs all foreign exchange transactions, distinguishing current account from capital account transactions. FERA treated violations as criminal; FEMA made them civil.

points.heading: Securities laws
points.text: The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the SEBI Act, 1992 govern the exchanges on which currency derivatives trade, the conduct of brokers and the clearing process. Currency derivatives are treated as securities for the purpose of exchange trading. Exchange bye-laws add operational detail.

points.heading: History of the market
points.text: USD/INR futures launched on Indian exchanges in August 2008, followed by EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR futures in 2010 and USD/INR options in October 2010. Cross-currency pairs such as EUR/USD were added in 2018. Each new product followed a joint RBI-SEBI decision, and the range of pairs and expiries has widened gradually as liquidity grew.

points.heading: Participants
points.text: Resident individuals, companies, banks and other entities may participate subject to RBI's rules. Foreign portfolio investors and NRIs can participate within the limits and purposes RBI specifies. Banks act both as members and as clients, under RBI's prudential norms.
