Each category has its own position limits.

points.heading: Underlying exposure rule
points.text: Under RBI's directions, users of exchange-traded currency derivatives should have an underlying exposure to currency risk. Positions up to a specified amount can be taken without documentary evidence, but the responsibility to have the exposure remains with the user. Check current RBI limits as of 2026.

points.heading: Product approvals
points.text: Exchanges cannot launch a new currency pair, contract type or expiry pattern on their own. New products and significant changes to contract specifications need SEBI approval, given in consultation with RBI because the products involve foreign exchange. This is why changes such as cross-currency pairs or weekly options arrive through joint circulars.

points.heading: Member eligibility
points.text: Trading and clearing members in the currency segment must meet SEBI's net worth and infrastructure requirements and employ staff certified in NISM Series I. Banks need RBI approval to become trading or clearing members. Certification must be renewed before it expires to keep dealing with clients.

traps: Naming SEBI alone as the regulator - RBI and SEBI jointly regulate exchange-traded currency derivatives.
Attributing RBI's powers to the SEBI Act; they flow from FEMA, 1999.
Thinking FERA still governs forex - FEMA replaced it.
Assuming any participant may take unlimited speculative positions; RBI expects an underlying exposure.
items.recap: RBI (under FEMA, 1999) decides products and participants; SEBI (under SCRA and the SEBI Act) regulates exchanges and members. A joint committee coordinates. USD/INR futures began in 2008, options in 2010, cross pairs in 2018. Members need net worth and NISM Series I-certified staff. Users should have underlying exposure.

items.title: Currency Derivatives Accounting and Tax: NISM Series I
items.description: Accounting for currency futures margins and MTM, option premium treatment, no STT or CTT, and business income tax on currency derivatives - NISM Series I.
items.intro: This short chapter covers how currency futures and options are recorded in the books and how profits are taxed. The key exam points are the margin and MTM accounting entries, the absence of STT, and the classification of profits as non-speculative business income. Tax rules can change, so check the income tax department's current position.

points.heading: Margin accounting
points.text: Initial margin paid to the broker or clearing corporation is shown as a current asset, not an expense. If margin is given as a bank guarantee or securities rather than cash, it is disclosed rather than recorded as a payment. Any margin shortfall is a liability.

points.heading: MTM accounting
points.text: Daily MTM payments and receipts are recorded in a mark-to-market account. On final settlement or squaring off, the net balance is transferred to profit and loss. For open positions at year end, the accumulated MTM reflects unrealised gain or loss and prudence may require providing for losses.

points.heading: Options premium
points.text: The buyer records premium paid as an asset until expiry, exercise or squaring off; the seller records premium received as a liability. On closure, the difference is recognised as profit or loss. Hedge accounting under Ind AS 109 applies to companies designating hedges.

points.heading: Hedge accounting basics
points.text: Companies hedging foreign currency exposure can apply hedge accounting so that gains and losses on the derivative and the hedged item are recognised together. This avoids profit swings caused purely by marking derivatives to market while the underlying exposure is not.

points.heading: No STT or CTT
points.text: Securities Transaction Tax applies to exchange-traded equity derivatives and Commodity Transaction Tax to commodity derivatives, but neither applies to exchange-traded currency derivatives. Trading costs therefore consist of brokerage, exchange charges, stamp duty, GST and SEBI fees. This makes currency trading costs comparatively low.

points.heading: Tax treatment of profits
points.text: Profits from trading currency futures and options on a recognised stock exchange are generally treated as non-speculative business income, under the same exclusion that covers eligible derivatives. Losses can be set off against other business income and carried forward. Check the current Income-tax law before relying on this.

points.heading: Hedgers versus traders
points.text: For a company that uses currency futures to hedge genuine export or import exposure, the derivative gain or loss is part of its business results and is usually recognised alongside the exchange difference on the hedged item. For an individual trader, the same contracts produce trading income or loss computed contract by contract.

points.heading: Expenses and records
points.text: Traders can claim business expenses such as brokerage and data costs. Turnover for audit purposes is usually the sum of absolute profits and losses. Keeping contract notes and ledger statements makes reconciliation and filing simpler. Tax audit thresholds should be checked each year.

traps: Assuming STT applies to currency derivatives as it does to equity F&O - it does not.
Recording initial margin as an expense; it is a current asset.
Calling exchange-traded currency derivative profits speculative income; they are generally non-speculative business income.
Booking option premium paid directly to profit and loss on the day of purchase.
items.recap: Initial margin is a current asset; MTM flows through an MTM account and goes to P&L on closure. Option premium paid is an asset, received is a liability, until closure. Hedge accounting matches derivative and exposure. No STT or CTT on currency derivatives. Profits are generally non-speculative business income.

items.title: Broker Conduct and Investor Protection: NISM Series I
items.description: SEBI code of conduct for brokers, KYC and risk disclosure in currency derivatives, SCORES, SMART ODR and Investor Protection Fund - NISM Series I notes.
items.intro: The final chapter covers how brokers must treat clients in the currency segment and what protection investors have. Questions are direct: which document must be given before trading, where to complain and what the Investor Protection Fund covers. Read carefully - several options often sound similar.

points.heading: Code of conduct for brokers
points.text: SEBI's stock broker regulations require brokers to act with integrity, due skill and care, avoid manipulative practices, maintain records, execute orders as instructed and issue contract notes on time. Brokers must not encourage excessive trading or make misleading claims about profits in currency trading.

points.heading: Client onboarding
points.text: Before a client trades currency derivatives, the broker completes KYC through a KRA, registers the UCC with PAN, and provides the Risk Disclosure Document along with the rights and obligations document and any policies on margin and square-off. The client signs acknowledgements.

points.heading: Risk disclosure
points.text: The Risk Disclosure Document explains leverage, the possibility of losing more than the initial margin, margin calls, the risk of illiquid contracts and the effect of exchange-rate volatility. It is meant to ensure informed consent rather than to discourage trading.

points.heading: Handling client funds
points.text: Client money and collateral must be kept separate from the broker's own funds. Brokers must settle client accounts periodically, upload client-wise collateral data to the exchange, and send statements so clients can verify balances. Unused client funds must be returned as per SEBI's running-account settlement rules.

points.heading: SCORES
points.text: SCORES is SEBI's online platform where investors lodge complaints against listed companies and market intermediaries, including brokers. Complaints are forwarded to the entity concerned and tracked to resolution, with escalation if the response is unsatisfactory. Brokers must respond within the timelines SEBI prescribes.

points.heading: Escalation and SMART ODR
points.text: A client should first complain to the broker, then to the exchange's investor grievance cell or SCORES. If unresolved, the dispute can go to the SMART ODR platform for online conciliation and, if needed, arbitration. Each stage has defined response timelines.

points.heading: Guarding against unauthorised trades
points.text: Exchanges send clients SMS and email alerts for trades executed in their accounts, and depositories and brokers send periodic statements. Clients should check these promptly and raise any unauthorised trade with the broker in writing at once, since delayed objections are harder to establish later.

points.heading: Investor Protection Fund
points.text: Each exchange maintains an Investor Protection Fund to compensate investors whose claims against a defaulting broker are admitted, up to specified limits. It does not compensate losses from market movements or from the client's own trading decisions. Claims must be filed within the period the exchange notifies.

traps: Thinking the IPF covers trading losses - it covers admitted claims against defaulting brokers only.
Skipping the broker and exchange and approaching SMART ODR first.
Assuming the Risk Disclosure Document is optional for experienced clients; it is mandatory for all.
Confusing SCORES (SEBI complaint portal) with the Settlement Guarantee Fund.
items.recap: Brokers must act fairly, keep records, issue timely contract notes and segregate client funds. Every client gets KYC, UCC registration, the Risk Disclosure Document and rights and obligations before trading. Complaints: broker, then exchange or SCORES, then SMART ODR. IPF pays admitted claims against defaulting brokers, not market losses.
